10038-the-magnetic-north:
Elizabeth Robins, writing as C. E. Raimond, published The Magnetic North in 1904, with a map of the Yukon country. It opens with a winter camp in the Yukon, a house-warming, two new specimens, a blow-out, and a shaman.

Later chapters follow a penitential journey, Kaviak's crime, Christmas, a Christian agnostic, Princess Muckluck, Holy Cross, the great white silence, and the pit. Robins writes of the Klondike world with a novelist's eye for cold, isolation, and faith. Readers get the far north as a place of testing, beauty, and moral choice.
10064-beltane-the-smith:
Jeffery Farnol's 1915 romance, dedicated to Frederick Hughson Hawley, follows Beltane the smith, who lived within the greenwood. Early chapters tell how he had word with the duke, Black Ivo, and how love came to him in the greenwood, with the love and grief of Helen the Proud.

Ambrose the hermit, Giles Brabblecombe the learned archer, a black friar, Black Roger the hangman, and three mighty men swearing fealty follow, with Friar Martin digging a grave in the wild. Farnol writes medieval romance with gusto. Readers get a lusty tale of outlaw, love, and loyalty.
10396-andy-the-acrobat-or-out-with-the-g:
Peter T. Harkness, author of books on circuses and how a great show travels, published this boys' circus tale in 1907. Andy, expelled from school and keen for a life of sawdust and spangles, finds his way to a big show. The book draws on real circus talk, routes, and work.

Hoop-la, disaster, a business proposition, and a first appearance carry Andy from Fairview to the road, with clowns, acrobats, and an arm of the law in pursuit. Billy Blow the clown helps him join the show. Readers get a lively, informed story of circus life for young readers.
10482-the-young-mother-management-of-chi:
William A. Alcott published this child-health guide in 1836, in a third edition much enlarged with a section on the mother's own conduct. Alcott, a popular health writer, aims to give young mothers plain, practical rules for the nursery, temperature, and air. The book was praised as among the most perfect popular works of its kind.

Chapters treat nursery walls, windows, and furniture, keeping cool, thermometers, stove guards, and the dangers of excess heat. Ventilation, oxygen, and carbonic acid from fires and candles follow. Readers get a clear, early American manual of infant care, dated in parts, but humane and practical.
10538-hyacinth:
George A. Birmingham published this novel in 1906, opening around 1850 with a drive to convert Irish Roman Catholics to Protestantism. Mission societies, elderly titled ladies, and young women collecting money poured funds into Connemara, where reports claimed converts flocking and schools full. Birmingham writes with irony and humor.

The leonine Archbishop McHale of Tuam, by his own policy, drove children into mission schools, while committees debated how to spend the money. Hyacinth, the heroine, stands amid faith, money, and Irish politics. Readers get a witty, humane novel of religion, reform, and Ireland in the mid-nineteenth century.
10541-children-s-classics-in-dramatic-fo:
Augusta Stevenson, formerly a teacher in Indianapolis schools, wrote this fourth-grade reader in 1908, turning children's classics into dramatic form. Stevenson dedicates it to Miss N. Cropsey, assistant superintendent of Indianapolis schools. The book lets children act stories, rather than merely read them.

Plays adapt Aesop, Grimm, Andersen, and Arabian Nights tales, from the travellers and the hatchet to the crow and the fox, the ugly duckling, the red shoes, and Ali Cogia. Each piece is short, clear, and stage-ready. Readers get a delightful, historic school reader for classroom performance.
10586-mike-and-psmith:
P. G. Wodehouse published Mike and Psmith in 1909, a school story about Mike Jackson and his remarkable new friend Psmith. Mike moves to Sedleigh, a small and undistinguished school, where Psmith's calm wit and grand manner soon turn routine school life into a campaign. Their chief opponent is Mr. Downing, a master who suspects them at every turn.

The plot runs through a fire brigade, a cricket match against Wrykyn, a stolen bicycle, and a long game of hide-and-seek with authority. Wodehouse keeps the tone light and the jokes quick, with Psmith stealing nearly every scene. Readers get an early, funny example of the author's gift for comic schoolboys and absurd plots.
1064-the-masque-of-the-red-death:
Prince Prospero locks his gay court inside a walled abbey to feast and dance while the Red Death ravages the land outside. Edgar Allan Poe follows the revels through seven colored rooms, where a masked guest in funeral garb appears at midnight. The prince, enraged, chases the figure with a dagger.

No sword can touch the guest, and when the mask falls, the court finds its own doom. Poe's tale runs a few pages, yet its images of plague, luxury, and time have lodged in the mind of every reader since. It stands as his most vivid allegory of death's reach.
10691-select-speeches-of-kossuth:
Lajos Kossuth, the Hungarian patriot who led his country's fight for freedom in 1848, won fame across Europe and America for his speeches. This volume, condensed and abridged by Francis W. Newman with Kossuth's own approval, gathers the speeches that stirred crowds far beyond Hungary. Newman compares the excitement Kossuth roused to the preaching of the First Crusade.

The speeches plead for liberty, justice, and national self-rule against the rule of emperors and kings. They show Kossuth's gift for turning political argument into moral appeal. Readers get the voice that made a Hungarian exile a hero in London and Washington, in speeches trimmed for English readers.
10959-the-visits-of-elizabeth:
Elinor Glyn wrote this 1901 epistolary novel as letters from Elizabeth, a seventeen-year-old girl, to her invalid mother. Elizabeth visits relations at Nazeby Hall, Eaton Place, Haviland Manor, and French chateaux, reporting cricket weeks, teas, balls, and suitors with bright, observant humour. A fall over a footstool at her first tea sets the tone.

Letters follow Elizabeth through London society and French country houses, where marquises, vicomtes, and jealous suitors compete for her attention. Glyn writes in Elizabeth's fresh voice, mixing innocence with sharp social observation. The novel charms as a portrait of Edwardian high society seen by a clever girl learning its rules, and it made Glyn's name as a novelist.
11165-wild-wings-a-romance-of-youth:
Margaret Rebecca Piper published this 1921 romance of youth in thirty-nine chapters. The book opens on a Northampton train at Springfield, where two silent passengers sit absorbed in newspapers: a rotund, rubicund man past sixty, foppish and accustomed to command.

Chapters follow Tony, Rosalind in Arden, a girl who could not stop being a princess, a boy who behaved like an ass, youth meeting youth, a shadow on the path. A heroine pleads for Alan, who has had nobody to guide him, against the Holiday tradition of what a man should be. Piper's novel follows young love, past mistakes, and second chances.
11167-deccan-nursery-tales-or-fairy-tale:
C. A. Kincaid published these Deccan nursery tales in 1914, inscribed to his little son Dennis, whose interest first induced him to offer them to the public. Kincaid explains the Hindu gods of the tales: Shiva the destroyer, Vishnu the preserver, Brahmadev the creative spirit, largely disregarded in practice, with Parwati, Mahalaxmi, Asuras, wood-nymphs, serpent-maidens.

Contents list the Sunday through Saturday stories, Mahalaxmi and the two queens, the island palace, Nagoba the snake-king, Parwati and the beggar-man, Soma the washerwoman, and Vasishta and the four queens. Snake-princes leave a necklace of nine jewels where milk stood, and never again bite anyone in that household. Kincaid's tales introduce English children to the Deccan's folklore, gods, and lunar calendar.
1129-the-tragedy-of-macbeth:
Macbeth, a Scottish general, hears witches hail him as future king and, urged on by his wife, murders King Duncan and seizes the throne. William Shakespeare's shortest tragedy follows the pair from triumph to guilt, madness, and death, as Scotland bleeds under a tyrant and Malcolm's army marches on Dunsinane.

The play's verse is terse and bloody, full of night, daggers, and sleepless guilt. Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking and Macbeth's "tomorrow" speech anchor its horror. The tragedy remains a staple of stage and school, and its lines have sunk deep into the language.
11426-the-call-of-the-north:
Stewart Edward White's Call of the North, a dramatized version of his romance Conjurer's House, opens beyond butternut, maple, pine, oak, and birch, in a land where shadows fall crimson across snow. A girl stands on a bank above a river flowing north, behind her a dozen whitewashed buildings, before her an interminable northern wilderness trodden only by trappers, Indians, and beasts. Once a summer a ship from England threads Hudson Straits to the Moose River.

White, author of The Westerners and The Blazed Trail, writes the free forest as both workplace and fate, with voyageurs, muskegs, and trading posts. The dramatized form tightens the romance for the stage. Readers of northern adventure will find its remoteness and seasonal rhythm its main power.
11623-the-dramatic-works-of-john-dryden-:
Walter Scott's life of John Dryden introduces the first volume of Dryden's plays. George Saintsberry edited the volume in 1882. Saintsberry praises Scott's Dryden as one of the best-edited books on a great scale in English. He faults only the revision of the text.

The volume gathers the plays with Scott's life of the poet. Saintsberry notes his own long acquaintance with the work. He first read it for pleasure, then for lectures at the Royal Institution. Later he wrote a monograph for Morley's English Men of Letters. Satire and the Green-Dragon Club are among the matters weighed.
11627-the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-0:
Grenville Kleiser's second volume of great sermons covers Hooker to South. It opens with Thomas Hooker, Cambridge fellow and founder of Connecticut. He was born in 1586 and cited before Laud in 1629. He left England for Holland, then sailed with John Cotton in 1633.

He led a migration to Hartford in 1636. Sermons in the volume run from Hooker's activity of faith to later preachers. A passage warns a runner for corruptible things to recall the devil, sin, and the world. Vain company calls him to stay, the sermon says. Biographical notes head each sermon, with an introduction by Lewis Brastow.
11922-minnesota-its-character-and-climat:
Ledyard Bill's 1871 book presents Minnesota as a health resort for invalids, with sketches of other places favorable to the sick, notes on health, and hints for tourists and emigrants. An illustration of Minnehaha, Laughing Water, fronts a work aimed at eastern readers weighing a move west.

Bill stresses the state's climate, its position at the head of two thousand miles of steamboat navigation on a single river, and the growing ease of touring the West. He also warns physicians to look beyond a cold itself to its causes, such as damp footwear. The passage shows how closely travel advice and medical advice were linked in his day.
11960-the-desire-of-the-moth:
Eugene Manlove Rhodes's The Desire of the Moth, with The Come On and illustrations by H. T. Dunn, opens with riders going hard and a cry of gentlemen, be seated. Its first chapter quotes a little song about Little Next Door. She loves the narrator more than her elders do, marvels at his tales, and says they shall marry when she is grown.

The song stops short, and the western story that follows tests that innocent promise against adult life on the range. Rhodes, a New Mexico writer, knew cowboy country from inside. His novel mixes romance, humor, and desert landscape in a tale where desire, like a moth to flame, draws its characters toward danger.
11997-crusoes-of-the-frozen-north:
The Crusoes of the Frozen North, from a story by Dr. Gordon Stables, opens with two sisters, Aralia and Pansy, gazing over the North Sea from a garden seat on a summer afternoon. Aralia is sure of one thing: nobody could have so good a time, or so strange an adventure, as the children are about to have.

An illustration shows Tom found at a lake-side, standing over a huge dead bear. Later scenes show Pansy crying with fright and happiness to an uncle figure, Staysail, while Tom clings to hope that a missing boat will return for his sisters. The story adapts the Crusoe pattern to northern seas and ice, with children, not a lone sailor, learning to endure cold, danger, and separation.
12013-my-year-of-the-war-including-an-ac:
Frederick Palmer's My Year of the War was written by an accredited American correspondent at the British front. It includes his experiences with troops in France and, for the first time in complete form, a visit to the Grand Fleet. Contents run from Le Brave Belge and Mons and Paris through Paris Waits, On the Heels of Von Kluck, Calais Waits, and In Germany.

Palmer describes the run to Brussels under Landsturm sentries swinging red flags as darkness fell, and trench life where working parties piled mud against chicken wire unless the Germans opened fire. His account, written for American readers before their country entered the war, mixes front-line reporting with reflection on what modern war meant.
12036-hygeia-a-city-of-health:
Benjamin Ward Richardson's Hygeia, A City of Health, published in 1876, imagines a city built on sanitary science. Richardson, a physician and fellow of the Royal Society, dedicates the address to Edwin Chadwick, acknowledging him as a sanitary student himself well read in Chadwick's work. Richardson calls the address a simple but hearty tribute.

Hygeia describes streets, houses, water, air, work, and food arranged to prevent disease rather than to cure it, with public health treated as a civic duty. Richardson's utopia belongs to the Victorian sanitary movement, which argued that clean water, fresh air, and decent housing would do more for human life than hospitals alone. It reads today as both a dream and a program.
12101-a-social-history-of-the-american-n:
Benjamin Brawley's 1921 Social History of the American Negro is subtitled a history of the Negro problem in the United States. It includes a history and study of the Republic of Liberia, and is dedicated to the memory of Norwood Penrose Hallowell, patriot, 1839 to 1914. Hallowell was born in Philadelphia on April 13, 1839, and the epigraph notes that these all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off.

Brawley, a Black scholar and educator, surveys slavery, emancipation, and Reconstruction. He also covers the twentieth-century struggle for rights, with Liberia as a parallel story of Black self-government. The book remains an early, systematic history written from within the community it describes, combining scholarship with a moral argument for full citizenship.
1234-organic-syntheses-an-annual-publica:
James Bryant Conant edits this volume of Organic Syntheses, an annual that publishes tested methods for making organic compounds. Each procedure gives amounts, steps, and notes from chemists who tried it. Organic Syntheses, founded in 1921, still publishes tested procedures for chemists.

The editors warn that some numbers did not scan correctly and advise checking the 1941 print edition before use. For historians of chemistry, the volume shows laboratory practice of its era; for chemists, it remains a source to verify with care. Conant, later president of Harvard, edited this early volume with care for detail.
12433-narrative-of-the-voyage-of-h-m-s-r:
John MacGillivray, naturalist to the expedition, wrote this narrative of HMS Rattlesnake voyage under Captain Owen Stanley during 1846 to 1850, published in 1852 under Admiralty sanction. The voyage surveyed New Guinea, the Louisiade Archipelago, and Australian waters.

Volume one adds the account of Mr. E. B. Kennedy expedition for the Cape York Peninsula. MacGillivray describes canoes with gunwales secured by knees, seams payed with black pitch, and bows closed by carved end-boards. The narrative mixes navigation, natural history, and encounters with island peoples. It is a classic of Victorian survey literature, valuable for science and for the human cost of exploration.
12481-hero-tales-of-the-far-north:
Jacob A. Riis, author of How the Other Half Lives, published Hero Tales of the Far North in 1910, reprinted in 1919. He dedicates his book of dead heroes to his living hero, Theodore Roosevelt, hoping many years pass before the last chapter of Roosevelt's life is written in the country's history.

Tales open with a knight errant of the sea and Hans Egede, the missionary to Greenland, and move through northern explorers, sailors and settlers. Riis tells their deeds in a warm, moral voice, praising courage, endurance and faith. The collection offers young readers heroic history from Denmark, Norway and the Arctic, told by a Danish-American who loved both his old and new lands.
12525-narrative-of-the-voyage-of-h-m-s-r:
John MacGillivray, naturalist to the expedition, wrote this 1852 narrative of HMS Rattlesnake, commanded by Captain Owen Stanley, during 1846 to 1850. The second volume covers discoveries and surveys in New Guinea and the Louisiade Archipelago, with an added account of E. B. Kennedy's expedition in the Cape York Peninsula.

Chapters describe Aboriginal tribes of Cape York and Torres Strait, warfare, social life, treatment of women, infanticide, education, scarifying, initiation, canoes, weapons, huts, dress, food, fishing, turtle and dugong. MacGillivray writes as a scientist under Admiralty sanction. The volume is a valuable, if period-bound, record of exploration and encounter in northern Australia and New Guinea.
12664-lyrics-of-earth:
Archibald Lampman's Lyrics of Earth, Boston 1895, dedicated to his mother, gathers Canadian nature lyrics. Contents run from The Sweetness of Life and God-speed to the Snow through April in the Hills. Forest Moods, The Return of the Year, Favorites of Pan, The Meadow and In May follow. Life and Nature, With the Night, June, Distance and The Bird and the Hour follow.

After Rain, Cloud-break, The Moon-path, Comfort of the Fields, At the Ferry, September, A Re-assurance, An Autumn Landscape, Snowbirds, Snow, Sunset and Winter-store follow. Lampman writes with a quiet, musical eye for fields, woods and seasons. The book is a fine sample of Confederation poetry, rooted in Ontario landscape and feeling.
12682-the-boy-allies-in-great-peril-or-w:
Clair W. Hayes's 1916 Boy Allies in Great Peril, or With the Italian Army in the Alps, follows Hal and Chester to Rome. Chapter one, The Brewing Storm, opens with an American lad of seventeen stopping his companion to stare at thousands thronging the approach to the king's palace.

Some mob, Chester, the lad says, and Hal agrees a real army could be recruited from the bunch. Most are soldiers anyhow, in Italy where military service shapes life. Italian Alps, war and boy heroics follow, in Hayes's brisk series style. The book carries the Boy Allies from France and Russia to a new front, patriotic and fast-moving.
12748-recollections-of-my-youth:
Ernest Renan's 1897 memoir looks back on a Breton childhood and a long path toward and away from the priesthood. He recalls the legend of the drowned city of Is, whose bells fishermen claimed to hear under the waves, and his family split between clerical and anti-clerical kin. Seminaries at St. Nicholas, Issy, and St. Sulpice form the core of the book.

Renan writes with charm about teachers, uncles, and a little girl named Noémi, while tracing how study loosened his faith. A prayer on the Acropolis caps his turn toward history and science. The memoir remains a classic of French letters, graceful, candid, and quietly skeptical.
12994-sydney-smith:
George W. E. Russell's 1905 life of Sydney Smith belongs to the English Men of Letters series and draws on memoirs, letters, and earlier sketches. Smith was a clergyman, wit, and reformer whose fame rested as much on his talk and essays as on his pulpit. Russell sets out to correct the dates and gaps left by Lady Holland's memoir and other early accounts.

The book follows Smith from youth to his years as a canon, and quotes freely from his famous letters on Catholic relief and reform. Readers meet the Peter Plymley letters, with their mock plea for a little light torture of oppressors, and the Mrs. Partington mop against the sea. Russell's portrait is of a humane, funny, and stubborn fighter for tolerance in a slow-moving age.
13114-the-collectors-being-cases-mostly-:
Frank Jewett Mather Jr.'s 1912 stories, subtitled cases mostly under the ninth and tenth commandments, turn on coveting and false witness in the art world. A ballade concedes the wrong of art collecting. Stories follow: Campbell Corot, on an able picture forger; the del Puente Giorgione, on a great lady and an artless expert; and The Lombard Runes, on seekers after truth.

Other tales tell of a cross that brings woe to a New York couple, a missing St. Michael found through a rude woodcut on the Quai Voltaire, and lustred pots of a grim sort. Mather's narrator meets dealers and collectors in Dieppe salons and Paris shops, where evidence grows by chance. The book is witty, learned, and sharp about how desire makes fakes and fools alike.
1319-increasing-human-efficiency-in-busi:
Walter Dill Scott, a pioneer of applied psychology, writes on increasing human efficiency in business, asking how firms can choose, train, and motivate workers well. The book applies psychology to hiring, advertising, and management. Scott, a psychologist at Northwestern, brought laboratory ideas into offices and factories.

Scott argues that attention, habit, and fair treatment raise output more than mere pressure. His plain, practical chapters helped bring psychology into American business, and they still read as an early handbook of management. His chapters on attention and habit still speak to managers who study how people work.
13282-the-island-of-faith:
Margaret E. Sangster's 1921 Island of Faith, dedicated to M's M and Chance, is a settlement-house novel set in a New York district bounded by Fourteenth Street and Delancey. Folk there seldom stray west of the Bowery or cross the sluggish river east. Sangster's chapters run from the settlement house and quarrels to Rose-Marie's rescue, a lily in the slums, and a happy ending.

Rose-Marie meets Jim, a jaunty young man with sharp eyes and a thin-lipped mouth, who surveys her coolly on entering a room. Ella bursts into the Volsky flat in anger, while Mrs. Volsky bends over wash-tubs and little Lily sits placid on Rose-Marie's lap. The novel is a warm, sentimental tale of faith, work, and love among poor city folk.
13402-the-hindu-yogi-science-of-breath:
Yogi Ramacharaka presents a complete manual of breathing drawn from Hindu yogi teaching, aimed at physical, mental, psychic, and spiritual growth. He begins with the claim that breath is life, then sets out outer and inner theories of breath, the nervous system, and the case for nostril breathing over mouth breathing.

Step-by-step lessons teach the yogi complete breath, its effect on the body, and seven developing exercises plus seven minor ones, with rhythmic and psychic breathing to follow. Postures, holds, and arm swings are spelled out in order. The book promises steadier health and clearer mind through daily, disciplined practice of breath alone.
1355-the-underground-city-or-the-black-i:
Jules Verne sets this tale in a played-out Scottish coal mine, where old Simon Ford still believes rich seams lie hidden below. A puzzling letter draws engineer James Starr back to the Dochary pit, and the two men soon find far more than coal: a vast cavern world, lit and worked in secret.

Below ground they build New Aberfoyle, a town of miners with streets, homes, and strange sights, while a mysterious fire-maiden haunts the dark galleries. The novel blends mining lore with wonder and peril. It is a quiet, curious adventure about industry, family, and a hidden world under Scotland.
13582-the-excavations-of-roman-baths-at-:
A paper reprinted from the Transactions of the Bristol and Gloucestershire Archaeological Society, volume eight, reports excavations of the Roman baths at Bath, with a plan of the baths as plate five. Leland, visiting Bath in 1530, describes the King's Bath and a sluice serving two places in Bath Priory once used for baths, now void for lack of springs.

Later work traced walls from Lucas's Bath, a base of sixty-eight feet, six or eight feet westward under a causeway to Abbey Green, pointing to the great Roman bath now familiar. Steps grooved by a circular sinking, four to five inches wide against the topmost riser, eased the dashing of water that annoyed bathers. The paper reconstructs Roman Bath from walls, steps, and old descriptions.
1366-the-cloister-and-the-hearth:
Charles Reade's great historical novel follows Gerard Eliot, a young Dutch scholar of the fifteenth century, from his home town through Europe to Rome and back. Love for Margaret, quarrels with his father, and a call to the Church pull him between the world and the cloister at every turn.

Through inns, courts, battlefields, and monasteries, Gerard meets rogues, scholars, and saints, and his long road tests faith, learning, and loyalty. The novel is rich in period detail and rough humour. It remains a beloved tale of a man torn between love and a religious life.
1397-the-ruins-or-meditation-on-the-revo:
Comte de Volney's famous meditation opens among the fallen stones of an ancient city, where a traveller broods on empires that rose and fell. A guiding voice then leads him through the history of peoples, faiths, and laws, asking why great states crumble while the same errors return age after age.

The book moves from ruined temples to the claims of priests and kings, and ends with a short Law of Nature setting out rules for human welfare. Written after the French Revolution, it speaks for reason, tolerance, and the rights of ordinary people against superstition and power.
14068-gordon-keith:
Thomas Nelson Page's 1903 novel follows Gordon Keith, a Virginia boy who loses his patrimony and must make his way in a changed South. Chapters trace his schooling at Ridge College, his work as an engineer, and his slow rise in New York business. Alice Yorke, glimpsed radiant in blue and white at a doorway, becomes the center of his hopes.

Duty and manners shape the story more than plot twists. Mrs. Lancaster defends southern courage to a puzzled Englishman, praising men who drove stagecoaches through mountains rather than sit idle. A hold-up, a ghost sighting, and a matchmaker's schemes test Keith's ideals. Page writes with old Virginia courtesy, and the novel charms as a portrait of honor, work, and love after the Civil War.
14080-custom-and-myth:
Andrew Lang's 1884 essays compare Greek, Indian, and so-called savage mythologies, dedicating the studies to E. B. Tylor. Lang attacks the reigning method, which treated myths as a disease of language, like a pearl from a diseased oyster. Colored, concrete speech, he argues, cannot explain why similar stories appear across distant peoples. Custom, rite, and older belief must enter the account.

Peruvian religion supplies a strong case. Every Indian claimed a pacarissa, or totem animal of descent, and sun temples still housed images of beasts once venerated. At Pachacamac, worshippers honored a she-fox and an emerald beside a high god. Hottentot tales add another puzzle, with a night spirit, a ghost, and a mantis insect sharing one name. Lang's essays stay lively and skeptical, inviting readers to test grand theories against stubborn, local facts.
14134-akbar-emperor-of-india-a-picture-o:
Dr. Richard von Garbe, rector of Tübingen, pictured Akbar's India for readers of The Monist in 1909, translated by Lydia G. Robinson. An illustration shows Akbar directing the tying of a wild elephant, after a tempera painting in Abu'l Fazl's history. Life and customs of the sixteenth century, not battles alone, form the subject.

Reform marks the reign. Akbar removed oppressive taxes on cattle, trees, and grain, regulated harbor and toll duties, and ordered losses from royal troops crossing fields to be calculated and repaid in 1574. Doubt tormented him at night, sitting outdoors on a stone, questioning the Koran's divine origin. Faizi and Abul Fazl brought Sufi teaching, shaped by Vedanta ideas of the All-One, against a narrow Ulema that used courts for enrichment. Tolerance emerges as policy and personal struggle alike.
14234-the-lure-of-the-north:
Harold Bindloss published The Lure of the North in 1918, issued in England as Agatha's Fortune. Agatha, whose father's canoe capsized on the Shadow, follows his last voyage with poignant tenderness, setting one day apart each year for quiet remembrance. She feels no shrinking, only gentle melancholy, as currents sweep past eddies and foam about half-covered rocks toward a grey trail of smoke.

Men of the north complicate her search. Father Lucien, watching light drive back dark, preaches spring as homily, while Thirlwell hates long nights and recalls a blizzard watch at Driscoll's shack. Black Steve Driscoll, dogged and sullen, holds a heart kindness cannot reach, yet stands as an uncommon type, not a rule. Bindloss writes Canadian wilderness with warmth and restraint, and Agatha's fortune proves less about money than about memory, courage, and love.
14661-conditions-in-utah-speech-of-hon-t:
Senator Thomas Kearns of Utah delivered this Senate speech on February 28, 1905, on conditions in Utah, addressing polygamous marriages and plural cohabitation. The speech was printed in Washington.

Kearns took up a resolution from Idaho's Senator Dubois for a constitutional amendment to prohibit and punish polygamy, and he argued that religion was not involved. He also examined Mormon Church bonds and tithes, noting millions paid since 1897. The speech is a primary document of the Reed Smoot era, when Utah's church and state relations faced Senate scrutiny. Kearns himself was a mining magnate turned senator.
15096-my-life-in-the-south:
Jacob Stroyer, born enslaved in South Carolina, tells his own life story in this memoir, enlarged and reissued at Salem, Massachusetts, in 1898. He writes plainly about plantation work, family life under slavery, and the war years that brought freedom. Early praise from ministers and mayors fronts the book.

Stroyer recalls masters, overseers, and fellow slaves with sharp detail, and he closes with his later work as a preacher and his hopes for Black Southerners. His voice is direct and earnest, not literary in the high sense. As a firsthand record of slavery told by one who lived it, the memoir remains a vital source for American history.
15195-rose-of-old-harpeth:
Maria Thompson Daviess's 1911 novel introduces Rose Mary of Sweetbriar, a hospitable Kentucky girl who cuts bread thick or thin to suit her guests. She laughs that nothing compliments a loaf like asking for a fourth slice, while Everett, perched on a stone table, begs care with her long knife. Illustrations by W. B. King match the fun.

Rose Mary's charm, kin, and Harpeth country life carry a gentle romance of home, courtship, and neighborly warmth. Daviess dedicates the book to her mother and grandmother, a sign of its family feeling. Readers who like Southern local color will enjoy Rose's wit and her wide, welcoming table.
1533-macbeth:
Shakespeare's shortest tragedy opens on a heath, where three witches hail Macbeth as Thane of Cawdor and future king. Urged by his wife, Macbeth murders Duncan in his castle at Inverness, and the crown he seizes turns to a reign of murder, guilt, and sleepless nights.

From Banquo's ghost at the banquet to Birnam Wood marching on Dunsinane, the play rushes toward Macbeth's death at Macduff's hand. Its language is terse, bloody, and supernatural. Macbeth is Shakespeare's most intense tragedy, a study of ambition that still grips stage and screen.
15357-the-notorious-mrs-ebbsmith:
Arthur Wing Pinero's play, set in Venice at Easter, centers on Agnes, a woman living under a cloud of gossip. She lodges in a faded palace on the Grand Canal with Lucas Cleeve, and the talk of other guests soon threatens both of them. The cast around them includes Lucas's wife Sybil, his father, a duke, and a clergyman.

Across its acts the play tests Agnes's past, her name, and her claim to respect. A friend presses her about who she truly is, and old secrets surface in drawing-room talk rather than in action. Pinero uses the Venetian setting, decayed grandeur and bright sun, to sharpen the clash between private feeling and public judgment. The drama asks whether a woman can outlive a reputation once society has fixed it on her.
15507-charles-duran-or-the-career-of-a-b:
The author of The Waldos published this Sunday-school tale in New York in 1850, through Carlton and Porter. Its hero is Charles Duran, and its lesson is plain from the title: the career of a bad boy, traced from homestead to deathbed, as the frontispiece warns. Chapters name each stage, so a young reader can follow the moral road step by step.

Charles grows up indulged, sulky, and set on his own will, then proves inattentive and unkind at school, where he is whipped and at last expelled. Idleness, fishing, hunting, and rough manners follow, with one vice leading to another. The book aims to alarm and reform: it shows parents their share in a child's faults, and children where disobedience ends. As a period tract, it is stern, direct, and earnest.
15524-digger-smith:
C. J. Dennis published this book of verse in 1918, revised in 1919, and dedicated it to the Australian Imperial Force. Thirteen poems, with a glossary, tell of soldiers and home folk in Australian slang verse. Titles include Before the War, Dummy Bridge, Dad, Digger Smith, West, Over the Fence, A Digger's Tale, and Jim's Girl.

The opening poem hears a woman sigh before the war, before the war, blinking back tears as she tries to smile. Later verses follow Digger Smith himself, Jim, the boys out there, and a man sawing wood, in the voice of ordinary Australians. Dennis writes in the idiom of the ranks, warm and rough, and the book stands as a popular Australian record of the Great War's human cost.
15591-a-woman-named-smith:
Marie Conway Oemler, author of Slippy McGee, published this novel in New York in 1919, with Grosset and Dunlap. A frontispiece shows a man telling Sophy he has found the lost key of Hynds House. The dedication goes to Elizabeth Heyward Oemler. It recalls an awful baby who bawled until her mother told another fairy tale. Now she bears herself sedately in dresses with frills.

Twenty chapters run from the scarlet witch departing and Ariel making music. They pass through the Hyndses of Hynds House, glamoury, and peacocks and ivory. They reach the judgment of spring and the forest of Arden. A jinnee intervenes, man proposes, and deep waters lead to harbor. Characters include Sophy, Alicia Gaines, Nicholas Jelnik, and Doctor Richard Geddes. Oemler writes a Southern romance of a house, a key, and a woman finding her place.
15879-elene-judith-athelstan-or-the-figh:
Five Anglo-Saxon poems in translation by James M. Garnett, formerly professor of English at the University of Virginia and translator of Beowulf. Ginn and Company issued the third edition in Boston in 1911. Garnett's versions aim at faithful, readable English for students. The poems span saints, heroes, and battles.

Elene, on Helena and the True Cross, leads, with Judith, the Hebrew heroine who slays Holofernes. Athelstan, or the fight at Brunanburh, and Byrhtnoth, or the fight at Maldon, follow as battle poems. The Dream of the Rood closes the set, with the Cross itself speaking. Garnett's book still opens Old English poetry to new readers: stern, noble, and strange.
15923-the-boy-and-the-sunday-school-a-ma:
A manual for Sunday-school work with teen-age boys by John L. Alexander, superintendent of the secondary division of the International Sunday School Association. Association Press issued it in New York in 1920, copyrighted 1913, with an introduction by Marion Lawrance. Alexander also wrote Boy Training and The Sunday School and the Teens. His book joins principle to method.

Alexander treats the teen boy's nature, his gang, his doubts, and his need for a manly faith. Lessons, worship, and recreation each get practical rules. The tone stays earnest and expert, aimed at teachers and pastors. The manual still shows how churches in 1913 tried to hold boys: not by preaching alone, but by understanding them.
16015-phil-purcel-the-pig-driver-the-geo:
William Carleton's Irish sketches open with Phil Purcel, a pig driver who never married and never laughed, yet stayed a general favorite. Friends knew Phil for a knave of the first water, but his grave face and feigned simple manners made his cheating seem almost a marvel. Carleton promises to explain that odd popularity, and the tale that follows does so with humor.

Two more pieces share the volume: The Geography of an Irish Oath and The Lianhan Shee, a fairy tale of the Irish countryside. Together they mix comic character study with folk belief and local speech. Readers get a short, sharp sample of Carleton's portraits of the Irish peasantry at work, at talk, and at mischief.
16038-great-epochs-in-american-history-v:
Francis W. Halsey edited this second volume of Great Epochs in American History, a ten-volume set that tells the nation's story through famous writers from Columbus to Wilson. Volume two covers the planting of the first colonies from 1562 to 1733, with an introduction and notes by Halsey. Its contents open with the founding of St. Augustine and the massacre by Menendez, then move through early settlements.

Each episode comes from a writer of its own age or a later historian, so readers hear many voices rather than one textbook tone. Maps and pictures support the text, and the notes explain hard passages. The volume works well for students and general readers who want America's colonial beginnings in vivid, first-hand style.
1606-kenilworth:
Walter Scott's Kenilworth, by Sir Walter Scott, Bart., follows the Earl of Leicester's secret marriage to Amy Robsart and Queen Elizabeth's glittering progress to Kenilworth Castle. Leicester, torn between his queen's favour and his hidden wife, leaves Amy in the care of the villainous Varney, with tragic results.

Through castle revels, court intrigue, and a murder plot, Scott builds a pageant of Elizabethan England, rich in costume and ceremony. Amy's fate gives the pageant its sorrow. Kenilworth is a classic Scott romance, beloved for its queen, its castle, and its doomed heroine.
16088-the-record-of-a-quaker-conscience-:
Cyrus Pringle's diary, introduced by Rufus M. Jones and published by Macmillan in 1918, records a Quaker drafted at Burlington, Vermont, in July 1863. Pringle was a young man of peace principles when the Civil War draft caught him. He spent a rainy day in his chamber writing and reading. He settled his mind for whatever might follow. The book prints his day-by-day account of that trial.

His entries weigh loyalty to country against loyalty to faith, and show a plain, earnest voice refusing to take up arms. Readers meet the war not on a battlefield but in one man's conscience, prayer, and talk with officials. The diary remains a clear, moving record of religious objection in wartime America.
16308-how-deacon-tubman-and-parson-whitn:
W. H. H. Murray's 1888 Boston volume, illustrated and published by Cupples and Hurd, leads with its title story of a New Year's kept by a deacon and a parson. Illustrations by Thomas Worth show Miranda the spinster and her Happy New Year handwriting. They also show the parson steering a sled and little Alice Dorchester begging him to stay. Old Jack, a horse of a great deal of character, appears too. The Old Beggar's Dog, The Ball, and Who Was He? complete the book.

Murray, the popular Adirondack writer, mixes humor, sentiment, and village character in short, readable tales. Deacons, parsons, horses, and children carry the fun. Readers who like old-fashioned American humor will enjoy this cheerful New England collection.
16337-from-capetown-to-ladysmith-an-unfi:
G. W. Steevens's From Capetown to Ladysmith, edited by Vernon Blackburn and published by Blackwood in 1900, records the South African War unfinished, as its subtitle admits. Steevens, author of With Kitchener to Khartum and In India, writes with an English alive and alert, praised for reaching the high-water mark of literature at Omdurman. His third impression carries the story from the Cape toward besieged Ladysmith.

War reporting, landscape, and soldier life fill the record, cut short by the author's death, which gives the book its poignancy. Readers of Boer War history will find vivid, first-hand journalism from a master correspondent. The unfinished shape itself tells the war's human cost.
16349-the-book-of-the-bush-containing-ma:
George Dunderdale's Book of the Bush, illustrated by J. Macfarlane and published by Ward, Lock in London, sketches early colonial Australia with truthful color. Its contents name squatters, whalers, convicts, diggers, and others who left their native land and never returned. The wreck of the convict ship Neva on King's Island, the discovery of the River Hopkins, whaling, and out west in 1849 open the volume.

Among the diggers in 1853, a bush hermit, two shepherds, a valiant police sergeant, and Gippsland pioneers follow, with government, law, gold rushes, and thirty years of change. Dunderdale writes from the bush itself, rough and vivid. Readers of Australian history will find a lively, first-hand anthology.
16463-in-the-shadow-of-death:
General P. H. Kritzinger and R. D. McDonald tell their side of the Anglo-Boer War in this volume, printed for private circulation in 1904. Rather than a day-by-day diary, they group events and notes from a wide field where Boer leaders often fought apart yet toward one aim. Portraits and diagrams illustrate the text.

The writers speak frankly as Boers who mourn the loss of the independence they took up arms for, while aiming to give no offense to honorable foes. Readers get a Boer commander's view of a long, hard war, in a book meant first for friends and fellow fighters rather than the general public.
16466-four-months-besieged-the-story-of-:
H. H. S. Pearse, special correspondent of the Daily News, tells the siege of Ladysmith from his own unpublished letters, issued in 1900 with maps and sketches. The story runs from the declaration of war and the battles of Talana Hill and Elandslaagte to the town's investment, the flight of its people, and the long wait under Boer guns.

Pearse writes as an eyewitness close to Sir George White's force, noting naval guns in action, nights of disaster, and the strain of a cut-off garrison. The letters keep a reporter's pace and detail. For readers of the Boer War, the book gives the siege as it felt day by day, not as later history smoothed it.
16517-liza-of-lambeth:
Somerset Maugham's first novel, published in 1897, follows Liza Kemp in Vere Street, Lambeth, a short straight street of eighty near-identical grey brick houses. On a broiling Saturday in August, the street fills with life as the heat eases, and Liza's story of work, love, and trouble among working-class Londoners begins.

Maugham writes with a young novelist's sharp eye for speech, street life, and social pressure. The book shocked some readers with its frankness, but its power lies in its plain human sympathy. It remains a vivid first glimpse of the writer Maugham would become.
16564-amphitryo-asinaria-aulularia-bacch:
Paul Nixon, dean of Bowdoin College, translates five comedies of Plautus in this first of five volumes, printed in 1916. Amphitryon, The Comedy of Asses, The Pot of Gold, The Two Bacchises, and The Captives fill the book, with an introduction, bibliography, and notes on the Greek originals of each play.

Nixon's English keeps Plautus brisk and funny, with footnotes gathered at each play's end. The volume serves students of Latin comedy and general readers alike. Roman farce, with its slaves, misers, twins, and tricks, comes alive here in clear, modern dress.
16679-the-history-of-england-from-the-ac:
T. F. Tout, Manchester professor of medieval and modern history, covers England from Henry III's accession to Edward III's death, 1216 to 1377, in this volume of the Political History of England. Chapter one opens with William Marshal's regency, John's death, Henry's coronation, the Bristol council, and the fair of Lincoln, with the sea-fight off Sandwich and the treaty of Lambeth.

Tout writes for general readers as well as students, building on new research since Lingard. The volume gives the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries in clear, connected narrative. Students of medieval England will find a solid, readable history of barons, charters, and kings.
16699-glen-of-the-high-north:
H. A. Cody wrote this 1920 Yukon tale, issued by McClelland and Stewart in Toronto and Doran in New York. He dedicates it to true men and women of the outer trails of the Yukon, where he lived and traveled for years. Chapters move from a fleeting vision and a fog bank, through the Great White Pass, to love against gold, a girl of Glen West, storms, plots, and rifles cracking.

Cody fills the north with comrades of the trail, prisoners, plotters, and cabins in the hills, all chasing gold or love. The glen itself stands for a hard, clean life far from town. Fans of old north tales will find brisk action, plain heroes, and a story that keeps its pace from first vision to final unmasking.
16719-the-husbands-of-edith:
George Barr McCutcheon wrote this 1908 light novel of marriage, kin, and social games. Edith stands at the center while husbands, a sister-in-law, distant cousins, a would-be brother-in-law, friends, and three guardians crowd her life. Each chapter adds a new relation with a claim, a plan, or a grudge.

McCutcheon plays the tangle for laughs, with brisk talk and neat turns as Edith sorts true feeling from show. The fun lies in watching a large cast press in on one woman and fail to steer her. Readers who like old society comedies will enjoy its pace, its wit, and its kind view of love under pressure.
16781-memoir-correspondence-and-miscella:
Thomas Jefferson Randolph edited this first volume of Thomas Jefferson's papers, entered for copyright in January 1829 in the Eastern District of Virginia. The title page, deposited by Randolph as proprietor, names the book as memoir, correspondence, and miscellanies from Jefferson's papers, printed at Cambridge by E. W. Metcalf. Four volumes make up the set.

The volume opens the great Jefferson edition of its day, mixing life story with letters and short pieces. It shows Jefferson as statesman, farmer, and thinker in his own papers. Readers who want the early Jefferson in print will find a rich, if old-style, collection, best used beside modern editions for its full text and its period view.
16782-memoir-correspondence-and-miscella:
Thomas Jefferson Randolph edited this second volume of papers of Thomas Jefferson, drawn from the 1829 set. It prints letters from London and Paris in 1786, including a note to Richard Henry Lee about new lamps tried in Paris and London. Public letters on a trade pact with Britain run beside the private notes.

Jefferson writes as envoy and host, mixing lamps, oils, merchants, and state business in the same plain hand. The volume shows the daily work of a diplomat abroad: small errands, big pacts, and news home. Readers who want Jefferson unfiltered will find letters that mix the mundane and the momentous with ease.
16783-memoir-correspondence-and-miscella:
This third volume of Thomas Jefferson's papers, edited by Thomas Jefferson Randolph, opens with a letter from Paris on July 19, 1789, to John Jay. Jefferson worries that Jay may have taken up an unfaithful channel for letters, since none from Jay later than November 1788 has reached him. He lists his own letters of 1788 and 1789, and notes that Jay's answer to one is known only through another person.

The volume tracks Jefferson in Paris as revolution brews, with letters that mix diplomacy, news, and personal unease. It shows a minister watching a great change while his own mail fails him. Readers get Jefferson in the thick of 1789, writing with care, candor, and a keen sense of how letters carry, or lose, the truth.
16784-memoir-correspondence-and-miscella:
This fourth volume of Thomas Jefferson's papers, edited by Thomas Jefferson Randolph, prints letters from Monticello in 1803 and after. It opens with a note to Levi Lincoln about a letter that came by post, which Jefferson will not answer in formal style. He asks Lincoln to pass his friendly view on by word of mouth to a captain and his friends.

The volume shows Jefferson as president and neighbor, weighing what to write, what to say, and what to leave unsaid. State craft mixes with farm, friends, and local ties in the same pages. Readers get Jefferson in his own words, careful, polite, and keenly aware of how a letter can act once it leaves his hand.
16810-black-and-white-land-labor-and-pol:
Timothy Thomas Fortune wrote this 1884 book on land, labor, and politics in the South, subtitled Black and White. His preface says he bases his views on personal knowledge of southern classes plus ample data from other writers. He believes Black people will yet win an honorable place in national industry and thought. He argues that laborers pay all taxes in the end. Lawmakers, firms, and syndicates victimize them, he says.

Fortune holds that wealth piled in few hands endangers government, and that land monopoly by persons, firms, or syndicates lies at the root of southern ills. His book is a bold, early Black voice on economics and race. Readers of American history will find a sharp, prophetic argument, still relevant for its case on land, labor, and fair play.
16857-probabilities-an-aid-to-faith:
Martin Farquhar Tupper wrote this 1851 book, issued by Silas Andrus in Hartford, as an aid to faith from probabilities. He takes the motto from Acts, where Agrippa says Paul almost persuades him to be a Christian. Tupper argues that certainty and prior likelihood differ: we know Cromwell and Napoleon lived, but a skeptic might ask if such men were likely beforehand.

Tupper builds his case from social states: anarchy breeds strong rulers, puritan zeal breeds bigoted chiefs, and so on, to show faith need not fear odds. He writes for doubters in plain, earnest prose. The book gives a Victorian attempt to reason toward belief, interesting now for its method and its view of history as a guide to faith.
16977-food-and-health:
This Lydia E. Pinkham booklet, called Food and Health, mixes recipes with ads and testimonials for Pinkham's Vegetable Compound and Sanative Wash. It asks if women read the little books left at their homes, and says they do, from cover to cover. Doses are given for liquid and tablet forms, and letters from women in Canada and the United States praise the compound for strength, sleep, and relief.

Recipes for tea biscuits, omelets, and scrambled eggs sit beside praise letters with names and towns. The booklet is advertising, not a medical text, and its health claims reflect its era's patent medicine trade. Modern readers should treat it as a historical ad booklet, useful for food history and for the study of how medicines were sold to women.
17112-many-thoughts-of-many-minds-a-trea:
Louis Klopsch compiled this 1896 treasury of more than twenty-five hundred short extracts, set out by topic for easy use. Nearly four hundred subjects get space, from ability and love to work, faith, and fame. Johnson, Longfellow, and a host of standard writers of many lands and ages supply the lines, each kept short enough to quote or ponder.

The book served speakers, teachers, and letter writers who wanted a fit line at hand. Its top order makes it easy to browse or to hunt one theme at a time. Today it works both as a quote book and as a snap of what late-1800s readers held wise. Dip in anywhere; the best use is a few lines at a sitting.
17196-life-of-adam-smith:
John Rae's 1895 life of Adam Smith follows the economist from Kirkcaldy school days to Glasgow College, Oxford, and Edinburgh lecture rooms. Early chapters cover his mother, his school fellows, and his taste for math, then Hutcheson at Glasgow, Hume as a friend, and a Snell exhibition to Balliol. Oxford brings a seized copy of Hume's Treatise, ill health, and few friends.

Later chapters trace Smith's lectures, his economic thought, and the road to Wealth of Nations, with sources and notes throughout. Rae writes in full, scholarly detail, yet keeps the man in view. Readers who want Smith the person, not just his theories, will find this the classic Victorian life to start with.
17210-the-adventures-of-my-cousin-smooth:
Timothy Templeton of Tewksbury tells the adventures of his cousin Smooth, Solomon Smooth, in this 1856 satire. Chapters follow Smooth in Washington, at supper and bed, in talks with General Cass, in dreams, and in Pierce's kitchen, where things stand sadly confused. A fish breakfast, a globe voyage, Downing Street, and a dinner with Citizen Peabody fill the later road.

Templeton writes in comic, mock-heroic prose, poking at politics, office seekers, and Young America. Smooth preserves rights, makes reflections, and stays right side up through each scrape. Readers of antebellum satire will enjoy a funny, talky tale of a plain man loose among presidents, lords, and diplomats.
17270-the-interlude-of-wealth-and-health:
This Malone Society reprint of 1907 gives the early English interlude of Wealth and Health, printed first in black-letter type. Speaker names stand in the text with marks around them, and notes explain letters with no modern match, such as a sign for with. The play itself sets Wealth and Health, with other personified figures, to debate and moral talk in the old interlude form.

The reprint, checked by Percy Simpson, rights upside-down type and keeps old spellings close. It suits students of early drama who want the text as it stood, with plain notes. Short and strange to modern ears, the interlude offers a vivid taste of Tudor stage morals before Shakespeare's age.
17411-historic-doubts-on-the-life-and-re:
Horace Walpole's 1768 Historic Doubts on the Life and Reign of King Richard III attacks the received black legend of the king. Walpole opens with a French motto on history resting on authors' testimony, and warns that writers copy one another or add to the original without new proof. Literary superstition, he says, makes readers treat any shake to an established character as profanation.

His method weighs each source's time, birth, country, part in affairs, means of knowledge, and interest in the tale. The book suits students of Richard III and of historiography itself. Short and combative, it launched the long debate over the king's reputation, and still reads as a model of source criticism.
17719-henrik-ibsen-a-bibliography-of-cri:
Ina Ten Eyck Firkins, reference librarian at the University of Minnesota, put together this 1921 guide to writings about Henrik Ibsen, the Norwegian playwright. The H. W. Wilson Company in New York printed it as part of its Practical Bibliographies line, for students and librarians who needed a map of Ibsen study.

Inside are lists of editions, an author index, a subject index, and an index to the characters in Ibsen's plays, with short codes for the journals cited. A reader can trace what was said about plays like A Doll's House or Ghosts, and where each piece first ran. It is a tool book, best used beside the plays, and a neat snapshot of Ibsen's fame in 1921.
17917-secret-band-of-brothers-a-full-and:
Jonathan H. Green, the reformed gambler, wrote Secret Band of Brothers as a full, true exposure of a powerful secret group in the United States. Green, author of The Gambler's Life, had turned from the tables to the lecture hall, and he vowed to unmask the gamblers' ring.

Chapters tell why he speaks now, who fights reform, and how men like Goodrich the gambler plot, cheat, and dodge the law. Green writes with the heat of a convert, and his claims run far past proof. The book is a lurid, old exposé, best read as a relic of the anti-gambling crusade, not as a sober history of crime.
17929-the-life-of-admiral-viscount-exmou:
Edward Osler wrote this life of Admiral Viscount Exmouth, revised and printed in London in 1854, and dedicated to the Navy. Exmouth, born Edward Pellew, rose from a bold boy to one of Britain's great sea lords, famed for daring, kind heart, and a dread of tyrants.

Chapters follow him from his first ship to the lakes of Canada, where he fought in 1776, built a bridge for Burgoyne's army, and nearly took General Arnold. Later years brought high command and fame. Osler writes with warm praise, and the book gives a full, old-style portrait of a sailor hero of the age of sail.
18032-the-canadian-commonwealth:
Agnes C. Laut wrote The Canadian Commonwealth in 1915, printed in Indianapolis by Bobbs-Merrill. Laut, author of books on the Hudson's Bay Company and the paths of the West, here asks what kind of nation Canada was becoming.

Chapters run from national consciousness and the tie that binds to Americanization, the rejection of reciprocity, the coming of the English, the foreigner, and the Oriental, and the Panama route. Laut writes with a journalist's vigor and a Canadian's pride. It is a lively, period survey of Canada on the eve of war, best read with later histories at hand.
18036-uppingham-by-the-sea-a-narrative-o:
J. H. S. wrote Uppingham by the Sea in 1878, printed in London by Macmillan, telling of the year the school spent at Borth. In the spring of 1876 and 1877, letters on the exile had run in The Times, and this narrative gathers that strange school year in book form.

The book is dedicated to Edward Thring, the school's second founder, and to the masters who held firm when health and order were at risk. Chapters open with exiles old and new, in verse of a fisher-prince and a found child. It is a quaint school chronicle, best for readers who love English public schools and their odd, proud ways.
18206-navaho-houses-seventeenth-annual-r:
Cosmos Mindeleff wrote this paper on Navaho houses for the Seventeenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, covering 1895 to 1896 and printed at Washington in 1898. Mindeleff argues that a people's houses show their mind and their industrial state more clearly than any other product of their art. Data on such early house forms, he says, were rare.

The paper describes the country and the habits of the people, then treats legendary and actual winter hogans, summer huts and shelters, sweat houses, and dedication ceremonies. Plates show a typical hogan, one in Canyon de Chelly, a summer hut, a lean-to, and a medicine hut. Readers get a detailed record of Navaho building, from winter earth lodges to the modern house of a wealthy Navaho.
18359-the-story-of-my-boyhood-and-youth:
John Muir wrote this story of his boyhood and youth, published by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1913, with pictures from sketches by the author. Muir, the naturalist who would become the voice of the Sierra, looks back to Scotland and to a Wisconsin farm, and to the nature that claimed him early. The book appeared first in the Atlantic Monthly.

Chapters open with a boyhood in Scotland: earliest recollections, the dandy doctor terror, deeds of daring, school and fighting, and birds' nesting. A new world follows, with stories of America, crossing the Atlantic, a new home, and a baptism in nature. Life on a Wisconsin farm brings oxen, ponies, snakes, fishing, and a narrow escape from drowning. Readers get Muir's beginnings: a boy made by birds, farms, and wild places, before he became their defender.
18366-the-challenge-of-the-north:
James Hendryx published this northern novel with Doubleday, Page in 1922. It opens in the fur department of old John McNabb's big store, where Oskar Hedin studies a Russian sable coat. Old John asks who in Terrace City could spend thirty thousand dollars on a fur coat, or twenty thousand on a black fox piece, and the talk turns to Mrs. Orcutt's coat.

Mrs. Orcutt bought hers in New York for thirty-five thousand dollars, lighter in shade and dressed up to look its best. Behind the coats lies a left-handed rivalry between McNabb and Fred Orcutt, neighborly on the street and on the golf course, yet unwilling to yield a ball to each other. Readers get a fur trade story where money, pride, and the cold north set the terms of every bargain.
18370-manhood-perfectly-restored-prof-je:
An advertising pamphlet from the Civiale Remedial Agency at 174 Fulton Street, New York, promotes Prof. Jean Civiale's soluble urethral crayons. The cover, sent only when requested and only when sealed, promises a quick, painless, and certain cure for impotence, lost manhood, spermatorrhoea, weakness, and nervous debility, as well as prostatitis and varicocele. This is the sixth edition, enlarged, revised, and illustrated.

The pamphlet calls its treatment the only standard and officially recognized one for diseases of the sexual and urinary organs, and cites Paris hospitals and medical journals of 1869. Readers today should treat it as a historical document, not as medical advice. It shows how Victorian patent medicine sold hope, secrecy, and bold claims to men who feared to ask a doctor in person.
18376-a-lecture-on-the-preservation-of-h:
T. Garnett, professor of natural philosophy and chemistry at the Royal Institution of Great Britain, gave this lecture on the preservation of health. The second edition, printed in London in 1800, opens with a dedication to Erasmus Darwin, whose medical and philosophical works Garnett praises. Garnett quotes Armstrong on health as the reward of rude and sober life, of labor, exercise, and temperance.

The preface notes that most medical gentlemen would agree on the main point: health is kept by plain habits rather than by physic. Garnett writes for a general audience at the turn of the nineteenth century, when public lectures carried science to the town. Readers get early health advice in lecture form: sober living, work, and exercise as the ground of a sound body.
18502-the-annual-monitor-for-1851-or-obi:
Printed in London in 1850, this yearly volume records the deaths of members of the Society of Friends in Great Britain and Ireland during that year. It opens with an essay on the group's falling numbers, noting that deaths had come to outrun births among members. Short obituary notes then follow for the men and women who died.

The essay weighs plain causes for the decline, from late marriage and marriage outside the group to the small size of the community itself. It also asks why the group's beliefs drew few new converts. For family and local historians, the book is a plain record of one religious community at mid-century.
18591-the-life-of-george-washington-vol-:
John Marshall, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, wrote this authorized life of George Washington, first published in 1804 to 1807 and reissued here in 1926 by the Citizens' Guild of Fredericksburg. Bushrod Washington, the president's nephew, chose Marshall and gave him Washington's letters, diaries, and secret papers. Marshall, who knew Washington from youth and served under him, spent seven years on the work.

This first volume opens with a survey of the English colonies from settlement to the war for independence, then begins Washington's life as commander in chief. A Trumbull portrait fronts the book. Marshall's life remains a landmark early biography, built on first-hand papers.
18592-the-life-of-george-washington-vol-:
John Marshall wrote this life of George Washington, compiled under the inspection of Bushrod Washington from original papers bequeathed by Washington, and published by the Citizens' Guild. Volume two carries the story of the commander in chief of the American forces during the war that established independence.

The volume opens with an introduction giving a compendious view of the English colonies in North America, from settlement to the war's beginning. Later chapters follow Washington through the war's campaigns, drawing on his own papers, and the book stands as the first great biography of the first president.
18593-the-life-of-george-washington-vol-:
John Marshall's authorized life of Washington continues in this third volume, reissued in 1926 in the Sponsors' Edition with the revised text. Its chapters follow the war through 1778, from the incursion into Jersey and the battle of Monmouth to the arrival of Count d'Estaing's French fleet. General Lee's arrest and sentence, the storm that scattered fleets off Rhode Island, and the siege of Newport fill the pages.

Marshall works from Washington's own papers, with care for dates, orders, and councils of war. A Gilbert Stuart portrait fronts the book. This volume covers the middle war years, when French aid and home disputes tested Washington's command. It suits readers following the Revolution year by year.
18594-the-life-of-george-washington-vol-:
John Marshall wrote this life of George Washington, compiled under the inspection of Bushrod Washington from original papers, and published by the Citizens' Guild. Volume four continues the story of the commander in chief and first president, distinct from volume two in this slice, which covers the war's earlier campaigns.

The volume's chapters carry the narrative through the later stages of Washington's command and public life. They stay grounded in his papers and in the introduction's view of the colonies. Readers who want the full Marshall biography will find here the closing movements of the war and the making of a presidency.
18595-the-life-of-george-washington-vol-:
John Marshall's authorized life of Washington reaches the presidency in this fifth volume, reissued in 1926. Its opening chapters cover Washington's second unanimous election, war between Britain and France, and his proclamation of neutrality. The Genet affair takes center stage, as the French minister's acts, the cabinet's views, and rules for ports in wartime test the young republic.

Later chapters follow Congress, debates on a navy and an embargo, Jay's mission to Britain, and the inquiry into the Treasury chief. Marshall builds the tale from Washington's papers, keeping a lawyer's eye on fact and order. The volume shows the first president steering a new nation through foreign storms.
18634-first-impressions-of-the-new-world:
Printed at London in 1859, this travel book gathers letters from a British family's rapid trip through Canada and the United States in the autumn of 1858. The writer, a mother traveling with her husband and son William, first wrote the letters for her young daughter. Friends later urged her to publish them, with only small changes and notes added.

The letters describe steamers, rail journeys over the Alleghenies, hotels, and daily manners, and they defend American hosts against harsher accounts by other travelers. William's lone travels, treated worse than the family's, get special note. The book reads as a warm, first-hand sketch of North America just before the Civil War.
18750-wandering-heath:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch published this story set at London in 1895, drawn from a reprint of that year's text. Its tales first ran in the Idler, the Strand Magazine, the Pall Mall Magazine, the Illustrated London News, and the Speaker. Titles include The Roll-Call of the Reef, The Looe Die-Hards, Jetsom, The Bishop of Eucalyptus, Visitors at the Gunnel Rock, and legends such as Flowing Source.

A prologue opens on New Year's morning with a poet grumbling that no one reads his verse, while his wife answers with gentle wit. Letters from Troy and two experiments round out the book. Q writes with Cornish warmth, humor, and a taste for sea tales. The set is a fine sample of his short fiction.
18863-the-loom-of-youth:
Alec Waugh published this school novel in London in 1917, with Methuen, and it was reprinted several times in its first year. Its hero, Gordon, arrives at an English public school knowing little of its customs. He learns quickly that games, houses, and the blue and gold ribbon of the Fifteen set the school's laws, and that a boy useless at games, like Davenham, counts for little.

The novel follows Gordon through lessons, friendships, rivalries, and the slow shaping of character that school life imposes. Waugh wrote from recent experience, and readers of the time recognized the world he described. Readers get a frank, lively portrait of Edwardian schoolboy life, notable as one of the first school novels to treat its subject without sentiment.
1894-visit-to-iceland-and-the-scandinavi:
Madame Ida Pfeiffer's Visit to Iceland and the Scandinavian North, translated from the German, records a woman traveller's journey to Iceland in the mid-nineteenth century, with explanatory notes and eight tinted engravings. An essay on Icelandic poetry from the French of M. Bergmann, a translation of the Voluspa, and a sketch of Icelandic history are added.

Pfeiffer notes the customs of Icelandic churches, where people cover their faces on entering, men with hats and women with handkerchiefs. She describes the island's farms, clergy, and weather with a traveller's plain eye. The book remains a valuable first-hand record of Iceland before tourism, written by one of the century's boldest women travellers.
18963-into-the-jaws-of-death:
Private Jack O'Brien wrote this 1919 memoir of war service with the 28th Northwest Battalion. He tells of leaving Winnipeg in 1915, training, and life at the front in France and Flanders. The book is dedicated to his colonel and the officers and men of his unit.

O'Brien mixes battle scenes with camp humour, punishments like confinement to barracks, and notes on comrades lost or wounded. Letters from his friend Bob Goddard add other voices to the tale. Readers get a soldier's plain, direct view of trench war, from jokes in camp to the road toward Hooge.
19058-ordnance-instructions-for-the-unit:
Issued for the United States Navy in 1866, this manual sets the rules for fitting war ships for battle. It covers guns, crews, shot, shell, and powder, with tables for officers, petty officers, and marines on each class of ship. Its tone is strict and practical throughout.

Later parts give care of guns and stores, checks each quarter, safe handling of fuzes, and steps for filling shells far from the magazine. Commanders learn what to inspect, what to report, and what never to allow on board. The book serves as a full working guide to naval gunnery in the years just after the Civil War.
19174-the-man-who-rocked-the-earth:
Arthur Train and Robert Williams Wood wrote this 1915 science fiction novel about a man who can shake the Earth itself. It opens with a stranger in Central Park who feels a strange drag, as if brakes were applied to a train, and watches Cleopatra's Needle topple and shatter across the drive. No one else is near.

The fall proves no illusion, and a hidden power soon threatens cities and nations with quakes at will. Scientists and statesmen must find the source before panic spreads. Readers get an early techno-thriller of secret science, power, and the terror of a weapon no army can meet.
19311-the-outdoor-girls-in-florida-or-wi:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this 1913 Outdoor Girls tale about wintering in Florida, in the sunny South. Betty, Amy, Grace, and Mollie leave Deepdale for warmth, while Will faces disgrace at home after a school hazing of Professor Cark. His father plans law work or a cotton mill job in Atlanta to teach him hard work.

Grace defends Will to Betty and Amy, noting her father's severity and her mother's view that firmness at the start is best. Florida scenes, friends, and scrapes follow. Young readers get a warm girls' adventure of travel, family trouble, and sunny winter days.
19465-draining-for-profit-and-draining-f:
George E. Waring wrote this guide to land drainage, first out from a New York press in the late eighteen sixties. It teaches how to lay out drains, make and lay tiles, care for drained land, and count the cost, then asks bluntly whether the work will pay. Later chapters turn to salt marshes, malaria, and town sewers.

Waring insists on thorough work at every step, from staking lines to fitting tiles round sharp curves. The book links farm profit to public health: dry land grows more, and dry towns sicken less. It remains a classic of practical nineteenth-century improvement writing.
19494-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Thomas Perkins wrote this guide to St. Albans Cathedral, with an account of its fabric and a short history of its abbey, for Bell's cathedral series. It walks through choir, retro-choir, and side chapels, noting altars to Our Lady, St. Michael, and St. Edmund, and a wooden figure of a beggar among its treasures.

Much of the guide deals with what was restored and what is new, a frank help to visitors puzzled by mixed stonework. Like its sister volumes, it favors clear facts over jargon, and it still rewards a slow walk through the abbey church.
19527-the-yukon-trail-a-tale-of-the-nort:
William MacLeod Raine wrote this tale of the north, published in the late nineteen teens. Gordon, seeking news of Sheba after two weeks without word from Kusiak, calls at the Paget house and finds her with the man she expects to marry the next week.

Sheba greets him with both hands out, murmuring pleasure mixed with fear. Raine's Yukon is a place of gold, trails, and tangled hearts, and the novel pairs frontier action with a romance that must cross pride and prior promises. The tale opens under the midnight sun, with four men playing pinochle on a river boat's upper deck.
19567-no-refuge-but-in-truth:
Goldwin Smith wrote this set of letters and essays on faith, evolution, and ethics, published in Toronto in the early nineteen hundreds. Most first appeared in the New York Sun, and they cover man's destiny, new faith linked with old, the scope and limits of evolution, and the immortality of the soul.

Smith argues that humanity may advance in excellence through many phases, yet never outrun its sources, as rays never outrun the sun. The book is a thoughtful late Victorian attempt to hold reason and religion in one view.
19667-an-essay-on-the-influence-of-tobac:
Few habits drew more ink in the nineteenth century than tobacco. An Essay on the Influence of Tobacco upon Life and Health argues the case against it. The writer pictures the user warping a form made with symmetry and elegance. In his words, the smoker can turn himself into something hideous. The tone is moral as much as medical.

Anti-tobacco tracts mixed health claims, religion, and disgust. They warned readers long before modern cancer studies existed. Some of their claims were guesswork dressed as fact. Others pointed, early, at real harms. The essay is a record of how reformers argued. It shows the sermon style that health campaigns once used.
19747-where-the-sun-swings-north:
Barrett Willoughby set Where the Sun Swings North in Alaska, and published it in 1922. It opens in a rough office at a northern trading post. A man with expert eyes closes his ledger with relief. He claps his hands, and a curtain at the side doorway draws aside. A small brown feminine hand appears through it. The scene promises frontier business and romance together.

Willoughby knew Alaska from years of living and working there. Her novels mixed trading-post fact with adventure plots. Gold, weather, and isolation set the terms for her characters. Northern fiction sold well in the 1920s. This book shows why readers trusted her detail. The ledger and the curtain sum up her two worlds.
1992-travels-in-england-during-the-reign:
Paul Hentzner, a German lawyer, toured England in the late 1590s as tutor to a young nobleman and wrote down what he saw. His account, joined here to Sir Robert Naunton's notes on Elizabeth's court, gives a foreign eye on Tudor life. Hentzner travelled as a tutor, a common way for young gentlemen to learn Europe, and his notes served later readers as a guide.

Hentzner describes London, the queen herself, great houses, and daily customs, while Naunton sketches the favourites who rose and fell around her. Together the two pieces form a firsthand window on Elizabethan England, useful and vivid for history readers. Naunton's court sketches add names and gossip, so the pair together give both street life and palace life.
19921-prehistoric-textile-art-of-eastern:
William H. Holmes studied prehistoric textile art of the eastern United States. The Bureau of Ethnology asked him about 1890 to prepare the study. It accompanied Cyrus Thomas's final report on mound explorations. The papers treat aboriginal arts shown by recovered relics. Textiles survive poorly, so Holmes worked from fragments and impressions. Cloth pressed into clay and copper kept its patterns after the fibers rotted.

Ancient Eastern weavers used twining, braiding, and early loom work. Holmes classified their techniques from the scraps that remained. His drawings reconstructed fabrics no eye had seen whole for centuries. The study appeared in the Bureau's Thirteenth Annual Report. It founded the study of prehistoric American textiles. Modern analysts still build on Holmes's categories.
20059-left-on-the-labrador-a-tale-of-adv:
Dillon Wallace wrote Left on the Labrador, a tale of adventure down north. Wallace knew the Labrador wilds from his own hard trips there. The book opens with verse on a life of storms and calms. Thorns sit among flowers, the poem says, yet we should stay glad as we can.

Inside, young travelers face cold, hunger, and vast empty country. Wallace writes of coasts and woods that few readers of his day had seen. The tale gives boys a true taste of the far north. Grit and teamwork matter more here than luck or ease.
20135-the-angel-of-death:
The Angel of Death comes from Swedish, in a translation printed at New York. It tells of Johan, a poet and preacher born in Dalarne in 1779. His father, a captain, led the Dalecarlia regiment in Sweden. Johan was one of a large family raised on modest means.

A poet-preacher's life in old Sweden forms the core of the tale. Faith, verse, and duty shape his path from a soldier's home. The angel of death in the title hangs over the story's mood. Readers get a sober life tale with strong religious feeling throughout.
20251-christmas-comes-but-once-a-year-sh:
Christmas Comes But Once a Year shows what Mr. Brown did at that season. Very cold, very bleak weather opens the tale in brisk strokes. The thermometer and snow fall fast as Christmas nears. Eggs and suet, by contrast, rise faster in price each day.

Everyone wishes everyone else a merry Christmas and a happy new year. Behind that cheer sit tight purses and hard choices for Brown. Holiday tales often test a clerk's purse against his family's hopes. Readers get a comic, touching slice of Victorian Christmas on a budget.
20294-a-handbook-of-health:
Woods Hutchinson published A Handbook of Health in 1911, a guide to the human body. He compares the body to an automobile before a long ride. A wise driver first learns how that car is built and fueled. He learns its gears, its tires, and how to cure engine troubles.
