So, too, should a person learn the workings of their own frame. Hutchinson, a doctor, writes in bright, plain, friendly terms throughout. Food, air, exercise, and rest all get clear, practical chapters. Readers get Edwardian health advice that still reads fresh and direct.
20305-marion-s-faith:
Marion's Faith, from 1886, is a novel of army life on the western frontier. A young officer jokes about paying for the clothes he wears. He glances down at his well-worn uniform as he speaks lightly. He prays they will be sent to reinforce Crook in Sioux country.

Out there, he says, no new uniforms are needed for scouting work. Crook, the Gray Fox, led troops in hard campaigns against the Sioux. Marion's faith will be tested by distance, danger, and duty alike. Readers get a frontier romance with a strong religious heart.
20309-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-in-:
Laura Lee Hope published Bunny Brown and His Sister Sue in the Sunny South in 1921. Bunny and Sue play in their backyard after a heavy snow storm. They build a big man of snow in the clean, fallen snow. Their mother let them out once the weather grew warm enough.

From snow at home, the tale soon turns toward the sunny south. Travel gives the Brown children new sights, foods, and friends. Each book in the series mixes mild mishaps with safe fun. Young readers get a warm trip south with two cheerful guides.
20388-report-of-the-railway-department-o:
When railways were new, the Board of Trade's Railway Department reported to Parliament on the lines being planned. This report weighs rival schemes for routes linking Oxford with the Midlands. Each line promised trade, speed, and profit for its backers.

One scheme ran from Oxford to Worcester and Wolverhampton, promoted by an independent company. It worked in connection with the Great Western Company. Together with the Oxford and Rugby line it formed one plan, set against competing routes. The report shows how Victorian Britain argued over steel, money, and maps before a single rail was laid.
20636-the-military-journals-of-two-priva:
The Military Journals of Two Private Soldiers presents the diaries of common soldiers from 1758 to 1775. One journal covers the French and Indian War, and the other reaches toward the Revolution. Private soldiers rarely left records, which makes these pages precious.

The editor believed the journals might interest American readers. They exhibit the everyday life of a common soldier in those wars which led to the founding of the republic. He yielded, he says, to the urging of friends and to his own judgment in printing them. Camps, marches, hunger, and skirmishes fill the plain daily entries.
20745-an-outcast-or-virtue-and-faith:
Virtue and Faith, sold also as An Outcast, opens with a bold claim about reform writing. The author says timid books hide real evils and lose all force. A cure, the preface argues, needs the cause shown plainly to the public eye.

That pledge shapes a tale of a cast-out figure tested by a harsh world. Vice, poverty, and faith pull at the lead figure across the plot. The book belongs to the earnest reform fiction of its century. Readers can see how such novels tried to move hearts and change laws at the same time, with story as their chief tool.
20795-the-cricket-on-the-hearth:
A kettle and a cricket open Charles Dickens's The Cricket on the Hearth, in this 1905 text. The kettle, one voice swears, began a full five minutes before the cricket sang. Mrs. Peerybingle's word rules the house, so the point needs care.

Dickens calls this tale a fairy tale of home, and the Peerybingles fill it with warmth. A blind girl, a gruff toymaker, and a test of trust deepen the plot. The cricket stands for hearth luck and kind hearts. Among Dickens's Christmas books, this one is the coziest, built for fireside reading in the dark of the year.
20913-a-woman-s-journey-through-the-phil:
Church and convento at Dumaguete, an old fort at Misamis, and bands that serenade guests fill the plates. Her Philippines travel book, from 1907, rides a cable ship that laid wire at sea. Markets, rivers, and street scenes crowd its photo list.

The traveller here sailed where cables linked far islands. She writes of towns, folk, and work with a keen, curious eye. Laying cable from native schooners shows the hard craft below deck talk. The book freezes the Philippines under early American rule, in vivid, first-hand travel prose. Few travel books of its day match its close, curious view of island life at work.
20941-american-lutheranism-volume-1-earl:
American Lutheranism, says F. Bente, is just Lutheranism in America, no fresh brand of faith. Doctrine, he holds, stays the same the world over, as does the church. Volume one treats the early history and the Tennessee Synod in that light.

Bente, a Missouri Synod scholar, traces Lutheran roots from colonial days onward. Synods, schools, doctrine fights, and pioneers fill his careful record. He writes to fix the facts of a church oft split by tongue and place. Church historians still use his volumes, written from inside the fold with a clerk's care for names, dates, and acts.
21037-the-cock-house-at-fellsgarth:
New boys tumble headlong into public school life in The Cock-House at Fellsgarth, and pay for it. Pocket money, hamper goods, and luckless freshmen all fall to old rule, Reed writes. Custom, immemorial and stern, owns the first hard days at school.

Fellsgarth's houses, games, feuds, and codes fill Reed's tale of school honour. The cock-house, top house of the school, sets the tone boys must meet. Reed knew this world from The Boy's Own Paper's vast readership. His Fellsgarth tales still stand as models of the classic British school story, brisk and fair.
21128-twenty-years-of-congress-vol-1-fro:
James G. Blaine, one of the most powerful Republicans of his age, published this political history in 1884. Volume One reviews the events that led to the political revolution of 1860, then follows Congress from Lincoln toward Garfield. Blaine wrote as a participant: he served in the House and Senate through these years.

Portraits of Lincoln, Sumner, Douglas, Stevens, and other leaders front the chapters. Blaine explains slavery politics, the Civil War Congresses, and Reconstruction from a Republican statesman's view. Statistical appendices back the narrative. The book remains a primary source for how Blaine's generation understood its own revolution in government.
21353-civics-and-health:
William H. Allen, secretary of the Bureau of Municipal Research, published Civics and Health with Ginn and Company in 1909. MIT biologist William T. Sedgwick wrote the introduction. Its frontispiece quote from Louis Agassiz claims a natural law is as sacred as a moral principle. Allen links the two in city government and schools.

Allen had led work on the physical welfare of New York school children. The book argues that health is a civic duty, not only a private one. Clean water, school inspection, and honest administration belong to one subject. It belongs to the Progressive era's push to run cities on science and records rather than patronage.
21397-manco-the-peruvian-chief-or-an-eng:
Peru, the old land of the Incas, is the scene of W. H. G. Kingston's Manco, the Peruvian Chief. An English family lives there under the shadow of Spanish rule. They watch a grand show from their country house as the tale begins.

The family is drawn into helping Manco, an Inca chief, flee the Spaniards. Kingston stresses how harshly Spain ground down the native tribes. A long trek overland brings danger from soldiers, snakes, bad bridges, and river rafts. Written in 1853, the book is among Kingston's first, and its style is already clean and sure.
21410-the-isle-of-pines-1668-and-an-essa:
Henry Neville's The Isle of Pines, first issued in 1668, tells of a castaway and four women on a lone island. The ship was bound for the East Indies when it was wrecked near a far coast. All aboard drowned save those five, one of the women being a Black servant.

The 1920 Boston edition pairs the tale with a long study by Worthington Chauncey Ford. Ford traces the Dowse copies and the Dutch, French, Italian, and German printings. He weighs who wrote the tale and how Defoe may have used it. Book lovers get both a strange early tale and its full print history.
21477-mark-seaworth:
Mark Seaworth searches for his sister and for his own true name in W. H. G. Kingston's Mark Seaworth. A calm ocean, smooth as a mirror under a blue sky, opens the tale. Moonlight makes a broad silver path across the dark sea in its early scenes.

Kingston tells the hunt through rich local detail and clean, fine English. The book was the first of his works put online by its modern editors. They praise it as a shining case of good writing throughout. Quests, sea travel, and slow reveals of kinship carry a story that many readers count among his best.
21500-memoirs-of-the-court-of-queen-eliz:
Lucy Aikin published her Memoirs of the Court of Queen Elizabeth in two volumes in 1818. Her plan covers Elizabeth's private life from birth onward. It adds the home history of the reign and lives of the great noble families.

Anecdotes of famed courtiers fill the pages, with notes on manners, thought, and letters. A front picture shows Elizabeth in the dress she wore to give thanks for the Armada's defeat. Aikin saw that England had many fine histories but few of this close, domestic kind. Her book still serves readers who want the court from inside.
21560-papers-on-health:
Professor Kirk's Papers on Health, first spread over eleven volumes, is here cut to one by his son Edward. The 1904 edition updates the doctor's advice where surgery and practice had moved on. Readers who want the raw text are sent to the full original set.

Kirk treats sore throats, fevers, diet, and the care of the body at home. Some practices he attacked had died out by the time of this edition. The editor owns each change as his own work and choice. The book preserves a famed Victorian health guide, whose plain rules reached many homes.
21790-the-dance-of-death:
Death comes for pope and peasant alike in Hans Holbein's famous Dance of Death. This 1903 edition adds a note by Austin Dobson. The earliest edition appeared at Lyons in 1538, a small quarto with forty-one cuts. Each picture carries a text from the Latin Bible above it. A long French preface addressed a noble abbess of Lyons, head of a house of wealthy ladies.

Holbein's woodcuts show skeletons leading away every rank of life, from the highest to the lowest. The images are elegant, sharp, and quietly funny about human pride. Dobson's introduction traces the book's strange publication history. Few picture books have been copied so often or remembered so long. This edition puts the classic within easy reach.
21895-the-old-coast-road-from-boston-to-:
The shore road from Boston to Plymouth is walked town by town in Agnes Edwards's The Old Coast Road, published in 1920. Edwards likens a city's story to a layer cake: cut down and every slice shows all the layers. Her road passes Dorchester Heights, Milton and the Blue Hills, and shipbuilding Quincy, home of the Adams houses. Louis H. Ruyl's illustrations and a map of the South Shore guide the eye.

Weymouth's romance, churchly Hingham with its Old Ship Meeting-House, and Cohasset's ledges follow in turn. Marshfield brings Daniel Webster's home, and Duxbury and Kingston lead at last to Plymouth. The book mixes travel, history, and local lore in a chatty voice. It is an armchair tour of old Massachusetts, made when the road still belonged to horses and memory.
21905-a-guide-for-the-religious-instruct:
Teachers of Jewish youth get a full course of faith in Isaac Reggio's Guide. M. H. Picciotto Englished it from the Italian in 1855. Reggio, rabbi and professor at Gorizia, was famed in the Hebrew literary world as scholar, philosopher, and elegant writer. His course moves in order: God, man, natural religion, and the need for revelation.

Numbered sections argue God's existence and attributes, then man's faculties, free will, conscience, and immortal soul. Natural religion is honored, then shown to fall short without revealed religion. The plan is rational and orderly, in the spirit of the Jewish Enlightenment. It shows how one great scholar thought the young should be taught to reason about their faith.
21999-the-wind-bloweth:
Ireland's passing world is mourned and sung in Donn Byrne's The Wind Bloweth, published in 1922 with illustrations by George Bellows. In his dedication, written as a prayer, Byrne says he chased the unbearable ache that is the mainspring of humanity. He worked through a race he knew best. They believe in Christ yet still believe in the little people of the hills. They love their own land, yet wander the wide world. He feared the Gaelic tongue itself was dying as he wrote.

Byrne had won readers with Messer Marco Polo, a tale of the East. Here he turns home to Ireland, to battle-loving people who always fall and always sing. The prose is lush and musical. The book catches a culture at the moment of its vanishing, and holds it beautifully.
22132-giants-on-the-earth:
Captain S. P. Meek wrote Giants on the Earth, a science fiction tale of revolt against alien masters. Giants from Jupiter rule the Earth through their viceroy, Glavour. The Jovians' huge bodies, bred for their planet's heavy gravity, dwarf ordinary humans. Earth lies under their yoke, waiting for a leader.

That leader is Damis, called the Nepthalim, who rallies Earth to spirited revolt. Meek builds his pulp plot on a simple contrast: giant tyrants, small rebels. Battles and escapes follow in the magazine style of the early 1930s. Meek, a serving army officer, wrote much early science fiction, and this tale shows the field in its raw, energetic youth.
22292-glory-of-youth:
Temple Bailey, one of America's most popular romantic novelists, wrote Glory of Youth as a story of young love and old houses. Miss Matthews, the companion, is glad to take the rooms just as they are. She was delighted to be asked to stay after mother died, the heroine explains. She loves the old things: the mahogany, the banjo clock, the embroidered peacocks, and the Venetian heirlooms from Dad's family.

Bailey sets that cherished household against the claims of youth and romance. Her heroines are modern girls with old-fashioned hearts, and her houses are characters too. The book has the gloss of the magazine fiction Bailey supplied by the shelf. It is sentiment, neatly made.
22424-frank-merriwell-down-south:
Frank Merriwell Down South, dated 1903, sends the famous schoolboy hero traveling. A dying man gives Frank the book's great clue at the start. Treasure lies in Mexico's Sierra Madre range, he says.

The spot stands one hundred twenty-five miles west of Zacatecas. Across a blue chasm, its towers and turrets glisten in sunshine. The dying man calls it a beautiful, dazzling dream. Frank Merriwell was the model hero of American dime novels. He was honest, athletic, and quick in every crisis. This southern adventure adds lost treasure to his usual tests. Readers get brisk period storytelling built for eager boys.
22500-the-works-of-william-hogarth-in-a-:
The Works of William Hogarth presents the great artist's engravings in series. Descriptions accompany the plates so readers can study each scene. A biographical search opens the inquiry into Hogarth's family.

His father's school stood in 1712 in the parish of St. Giles. In that parish register, searchers hoped to find his death recorded. The register was searched, the account says, to no purpose. Such detective work frames the edition's care for facts. Hogarth's own prints need less help: they satirize English life brilliantly. Rakes, elections, and marriages unfold panel by panel in his lines. Readers get both the pictures and period commentary. Together they preserve Georgian England laughing at itself.
22735-king-of-the-jews-a-story-of-christ:
William T. Stead adapted King of the Jews from the Oberammergau Passion Play, telling the story of Christ's last days on earth; the book appeared in 1900. Stead, the famous campaigning journalist, shaped the Bavarian villagers' play into a narrative for English readers who would never see the original.

The sample shows the entry into Jerusalem: amid the jubilant crowd, Jesus appeared in a long gray garment with a flowing robe cast over it. His face was calm and thoughtful. Sun had darkened his long black hair and beard. He rode on a colt that looked nearly too small to bear his weight. Stead writes reverently and vividly, scene by scene. The book carried the Passion Play's fame around the English-speaking world.
22764-on-the-origin-of-species-by-means-:
Charles Darwin wrote On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, the 1859 book that changed biology forever. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Darwin argues that species arise from earlier species, shaped over ages by natural selection acting on small variations, as breeders shape pigeons and dogs.

His introduction recalls the voyage of the Beagle. Facts about the distribution of South America's inhabitants first struck him there. So did the relations of present to past life on that continent. Those facts, he writes, seemed to throw light on the origin of species. One great philosopher had called that problem the mystery of mysteries. The book that grew from them marshals geology, breeding, and island life into one vast argument. No summary can replace reading the argument itself, still lucid and bold.
23129-the-young-voyageurs-boy-hunters-in:
Thomas Mayne Reid outfits his hunters in The Young Voyageurs, boy hunters in the North. A vast journey it will be, the narrator warns. It will cost many thousand miles of travel. No train, steamboat, stagecoach, or even a horse will carry them, the narrator warns. No hotel board or roadside inn waits along their route either.

Reid's boys travel by canoe and snowshoe through the fur country, hunting to eat and learning the North animal by animal. His books mixed adventure with real natural history, and young readers trusted both. The voyageurs of the title were the French-Canadian boatmen of the trade, and the boys apprentice themselves to that hard school. Few period series reward rereading like Reid's.
23319-mechanical-drawing-self-taught-com:
Joshua Rose wrote this self-teaching guide to mechanical drawing, published in Philadelphia with more than three hundred engravings. It teaches how to choose and prepare drawing tools, then gives elementary practice in geometry and mechanism.

Screw threads, gear wheels, motions, engines, and boilers all appear as examples, so a student learns by drawing real machine parts. Rose, author of works for machinists, wrote for workers who needed skill without a school, and his book served them for decades. Rose wrote for workers who needed skill without a school to teach them. A lathe passage measures a diameter by running the eye along an inch line to its meeting with a 45-degree line.
23325-seth:
Frances Hodgson Burnett placed this tale in Black Creek, a small East Tennessee town newly reached by a rail line to the mines. Seth arrives at dusk on an empty coal train, dusty and tired, with all he owns tied in a small bundle on a stick.

Few strangers reach the town, so his arrival stirs talk among the loungers at the depot and the Welsh and English miners who work the pits. The story follows the young newcomer as he finds work, meets the town folk, and learns the rough codes of a mining place. Burnett draws the town in close detail, from its depot shed to its talk, songs, and quarrels.
23426-the-last-place-on-earth:
Jim Harmon wrote this science fiction tale of Sam Collins, a rangy young man on a small town Main Street at dusk, where false fronts spill shadow and heat soaks through denim. The town undertaker, old Doc Candle in endless black, greets Sam with a grave joke: he means to bury him one day.

Sam laughs it off, for Candle has never joked before, but the words hang in the twilight air like a warning. Harmon writes the street in vivid, slightly off kilter detail, with shop windows rippled by sunset and hair rising on Sam's neck. The tale teases a strangeness under plain town life, and readers who like a short, eerie science fiction setup will enjoy its sly humour and its chill close.
23457-the-keepsake-or-poems-and-pictures:
Darton, Harvey, and Darton printed this keepsake in London in eighteen eighteen, a book of poems and pictures for childhood and youth. A frontispiece of Richard and his brother opens the set, with verses on sleepy Mary, Mary's lesson, impatient Julia, the cuckoo, red shoes and black shoes, and the gardeners.

Little girls and boys, a blind boy, and the four seasons follow, with Anne and Edward, George and Edmund, Fanny, Alfred, and William in turn. The verse stays simple and kind, made for reading aloud and for learning by heart. Parents and collectors will enjoy the book as a charming relic of Regency childhood, where poems teach manners, patience, and love of home in gentle rhymes.
23536-hatty-and-marcus-or-first-steps-in:
Aunt Friendly wrote this eighteen fifty nine moral tale for children, printed by Anson D. F. Randolph of New York. Hatty Lee, ten years old, returns from a visit to her grandmother to a home in happy disorder, as brothers and sister, wild with delight, struggle to keep order for their favourite.

Marcus, two years older and sure he is almost a man, leads the welcome, and Aunt Barbara's picture fronts the book. The tale follows Hatty and Marcus through small trials, temptations, and kind choices, each step a first step on the better path of the title. Young readers will enjoy the family warmth and the plain lessons, while grown readers will note the gentle, mid century style of children's moral fiction.
23608-the-day-of-wrath:
Maurus Jokai wrote this Hungarian novel, translated by R. Nisbet Bain and printed in nineteen hundred by Doubleday, Page, under the title The Day of Wrath. Its Hungarian title, Szomoru Napok, means sad days, and the preface says it was written in the darkest days of Jokai's life, under unmerited misfortune.

Chapters move from a bird of ill omen and a headsman's family through a childish malefactor, a divine visitation, and an unbeloved son. Two famous pedagogues, a man of iron, a Polish woman, and a plague follow, toward a leader of the people, a first spark, fire, a leather bell, and a sentence of death. Jokai writes with generous, sanguine force even in gloom, making a sweeping tale of Hungary, justice, and wrath. Readers of European fiction will find a rich, stormy novel of fate and revolt.
23736-the-dew-of-their-youth:
S. R. Crockett published The Dew of Their Youth in London in 1910, a novel of Scottish life told across two parts. Part One opens at the haunted house of Marnhoul, with Miss Irma holding audiences, a censor of morals on patrol, and Agnes Anne turning spy. A crowbar in the wood and a fight in the dark raise the stakes.

Part Two brings a grandmother speaking her mind, Castle Connoway, and the real Mr. Poole, with loaded-pistol Pollixfen along the way. Crockett, author of The Lilac Sunbonnet and The Black Douglas, writes of youth, village gossip, and old houses with secrets. The dew of the title is the freshness of young days, recalled by older eyes.
23739-the-life-of-mansie-wauch-tailor-in:
D. M. Moir edited The Life of Mansie Wauch, Tailor in Dalkeith, in a 1911 edition with color pictures by Charles Martin Hardie. Mansie writes his own life, or claims to, and Moir presents sketches principally of humble Scottish character, dedicating them to John Galt, author of Annals of the Parish.

Mansie's preliminaries explain his plan. Like all notable characters, he will commit to paper the surprising occurrences of his life, so that those who come after may take warning and be benefited. Friends urged him on, chief among them James Batter, a true judge of book-learning. The result is a Scots classic of village humor, told in Mansie's own voice.
23916-blue-bonnet-in-boston-or-boarding-:
Caroline E. Jacobs and Lela H. Richards published Blue Bonnet in Boston in 1914, a sequel to A Texas Blue Bonnet and Blue Bonnet's Ranch Party. The Texas girl goes to boarding school at Miss North's, and the book ran through eleven impressions by 1921.

Chapters follow the We Are Sevens, a week-end, and a surprise, through boarding-school days, new friends, trouble, and penance. Woodford, a cloud, and its lifting lead to initiation, settlement work, and a Harvard tea. Kitty's cotillion brings the frontispiece moment, when Blue Bonnet wrenches a whip from Alec's hand. It closes with a junior spread, a lambs' frolic, and commencement.
2442-history-of-the-impeachment-of-andre:
Edmund G. Ross, the Kansas senator whose vote saved Andrew Johnson, writes the history of the president's impeachment. The book follows Johnson's clash with Congress over Reconstruction, the Tenure of Office Act, and the Senate trial that acquitted him by one vote. Ross writes with insider knowledge and a defense of his own decisive stand.

The history's perspective is partisan, as its author's role demands, but its detail is invaluable. Readers of Civil War and Reconstruction politics will find a key primary account. The trial's drama still grips. Ross's vote against conviction made him famous and cost him his Senate seat.
2443-the-story-of-the-mormons-from-the-d:
William Alexander Linn's Story of the Mormons traces the faith from Joseph Smith's visions to the settlement of Utah and the controversies of polygamy. The history covers the church's founding, its persecutions, its westward trek, and its clash with the United States government, written from a critical, non-Mormon viewpoint. Linn draws on documents and testimony.

The book's early twentieth century perspective shapes its judgments, and modern readers should pair it with Mormon and scholarly accounts. As a contemporary history, it remains detailed and readable. Students of American religion will find a substantial survey.
24438-from-fort-henry-to-corinth:
M. F. Force, late brigadier-general of United States Volunteers, commanding the First Division of the Seventeenth Corps, wrote this second volume of Campaigns of the Civil War, From Fort Henry to Corinth. It was published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York. This text is a facsimile reprint of the 1881 to 1883 edition, issued by the Archive Society in 1992. Force says he prepared the narrative from authentic material, contemporary with the events.

His main source is the official battle and operation reports, National and Confederate, in the Military Reports volumes under Colonel Scott of the War Records Office. Document Number 66, printed by Senate resolution in the Thirty-seventh Congress, holds casualty reports and lists of killed, wounded, and missing. These are not in the Military Reports volumes. Battle reports of the Twentieth and Fifty-third Ohio at Shiloh, never printed, serve him. Readers get the campaigns, from the records.
24487-the-story-of-pocahontas-and-captai:
E. Boyd Smith both told and pictured this children's history, published at Boston and New York in 1906. Coloured plates follow the story from John Smith's early adventures to the landing of the colonists in 1607. Smith is ambushed, taken prisoner, and saved, the plates tell us, by Pocahontas.

Later plates show Pocahontas bringing food to the starving colonists, warning Smith, and being captured by Argall, before her marriage and voyage to England. Smith's pictures give the old tale a vivid, pageant-like form. Young readers get a romantic version of the Jamestown story, as Americans told it at the start of the twentieth century.
24517-accidental-death:
Peter Baily wrote this short science-fiction story, first printed in a 1950s magazine and illustrated by Schoenherr. It opens on a frozen wilderness, where wind screams over ice slabs and a thing of metal and plastics lies at the end of a long furrow in the snow. Something has fallen, or been thrown down, in a dead and empty place.

The story that follows turns on a weapon nobody knows is loaded, as its title warns. Baily builds suspense from a stark Arctic scene and a single dangerous object. Readers get a tight, chilling tale of accident and intent, short enough to read at one sitting and sharp enough to linger after.
24679-lilith:
Ada Langworthy Collier wrote this poem on Lilith, the legend of the first woman, published at Boston in 1885. Her preface explains the Rabbinic speculation behind it. Eve was Adam's second wife, and the double account of woman's creation in Genesis points to an earlier wife. That wife was named Lilith, expelled from Eden before Eve was made.

Collier retells the legend in verse, drawing on commentators such as Abraham Ecchelensis. Her Lilith is proud, wilful, and banished, a figure of female independence long before her time. Readers interested in myth, poetry, and women's history will find this Victorian poem a striking early telling of Lilith's story.
24762-diggers-in-the-earth:
Eva March Tappan wrote this school reader in 1916 as the second book of her Industrial Readers series. Eleven short chapters explain how people get useful stuff from the earth: coal mines, stone quarries, sand, brick works, gold diggings, silver, iron, copper, aluminum, oil, and salt. Each chapter tells the story of one material in plain words.

Young readers learn how coal formed from ancient plants, how miners thaw frozen ground with steam in Alaska, and how a gold vein can widen, narrow, and vanish. Tappan keeps the focus on real work and real workers. The book still serves as a clear first look at mining and the raw stuff of daily life.
24886-an-account-of-the-foxglove-and-som:
William Withering, a Birmingham hospital doctor, published his Account of the Foxglove in 1785. After ten years of cautious use, he set down every case in which he gave the plant, good or bad, rather than cherry-picking successes. His subject is dropsy, the swelling of body and limbs, and the foxglove's power to drain it.

Cases fill the book: a large man struck by palsy whose swollen legs subsided on small doses of digitalis infusion, and a hard drinker whose belly dropsy eased under the same care. Withering warns plainly that the drug is strong and must be watched. The book founded the modern use of digitalis for the heart.
24891-stray-leaves-from-an-arctic-journa:
Lieutenant Sherard Osborn, commanding H.M.S. Pioneer, published these stray leaves from an Arctic journal in New York in 1852. The book covers eighteen months in the polar regions in 1850 and 1851, searching for Sir John Franklin's lost expedition, and it is dedicated to Lady Franklin.

Osborn tells how his party found Franklin's first winter quarters, dated to the winter of 1845-46. That news dashed fears that the ships had sunk in Baffin's Bay on their way out. The journal mixes ice, sledge work, and sailor feeling for the missing men. It gives a vivid, firsthand record of the Franklin search at its height.
25041-humour-of-the-north:
Lawrence J. Burpee's Humour of the North, published by the Musson Book Company of Toronto in 1912, gathers representative Canadian wit and humour. Burpee admits a fuller editor might someday glean the whole field, from Haliburton and Lanigan to anonymous jokes in Grip, Punch in Canada, the Grumbler, the Free Lance, and Diogenes. Speeches by McGee, Howe, and Davin would join them. His little collection makes no such ambitious claim, offering instead familiar examples from better known writers.

Sources are credited throughout: Howe from Poems and Essays, Haliburton from The Old Judge, Drummond from The Habitant, Johnnie Courteau, and The Voyageur, Mrs. Cotes from Social Departure, and DeMille from The Dodge Club. One sketch gives us an unaggressive reporter whose boots and hat alone suggest journalism, greeting his hosts with amiability while Orthodocia flees to the window. The book is a friendly tour of northern humor.
25075-a-letter-from-major-robert-carmich:
Major Robert Carmichael-Smyth's 1849 Letter to his friend, the author of The Clockmaker, argues for a British colonial railway across North America. The line would run from Halifax in Nova Scotia to the mouth of the Fraser River on the Pacific coast. Writing before any such line existed, Carmichael-Smyth treats the scheme as practical, not fanciful.

He answers skeptics by recalling how steam navigation itself was once called impossible, then sets out the trade, settlement, and defense gains a continental railway would bring. The pamphlet is an early statement of the transcontinental idea, published two decades before Canada's own railway debates made it national policy.
25189-the-idler-magazine-volume-iii-june:
The June 1893 number of the Idler Magazine opens with the second part of Sophie Wassilieff's Memoirs of a Female Nihilist, describing twenty-seven months in a fortress prison. Her cell, ten feet square with whitewashed stone walls, holds only a stool and rough furniture.

Other pieces include Kipling's Legs of Sister Ursula, a visit to Emile Zola in his den, R. M. Ballantyne on his first book, and an Ethiopian cricket match by Eden Phillpotts. The Idlers Club debates whether Britain should have a dramatic academy. The issue shows the Idler at its most varied and sociable.
25205-light-on-the-child-s-path:
William A. Bixler's Light on the Child's Path, published by the Warner Press in 1918, is a children's religious reader. Its short chapters and poems move from creation and the Garden of Eden through the life of Jesus to prayer, kindness, and country life.

Parables retold for children include the Sower, the Leaven, the Laborers in the Vineyard, and the Wheat and Tares. Nature pieces on birds, animals, flowers, and seasons sit beside lessons on visiting the sick and being kind to the aged. The book was made for home and Sunday-school reading in plain, simple language.
25372-the-idler-magazine-volume-iii-july:
The July 1893 number of the Idler Magazine opens with Jerome K. Jerome's Woman of the Saeter, a Norwegian tale of reindeer stalking. A young guide leads the traveler to a desolate upland hut, where coffee and dried fish precede a damp dawn with a Remington rifle.

Other pieces include Marie Adelaide Belloc on Alphonse Daudet at home, Robert Buchanan's Dismal Throng, and I. Zangwill on his first book. Sophie Wassilieff continues her nihilist memoirs with one day in prison, and the Idlers Club debates tipping. The issue keeps the Idler's easy mix of travel, letters, and club talk.
25426-broad-grins-comprising-with-new-ad:
George Colman the Younger's Broad Grins, in an eighth edition from 1839, gathers comic tales in verse, with new additions to those formerly called My Night-Gown and Slippers. Colman prints at his own risk and jokes with his booksellers, Cadell and Davies, who call three tales too short a work.

Verses tell of a knight who knocked down a friar. He then wakes his ale-drunk man by pulling his nose, as one pulls the wire between a doll's wooden thighs to open its eyes. Draughts of hops and malt, snoring like twenty thousand hogs, and a Duke of Limbs seized by the proboscis complete the broad humor. The book is Georgian fun in verse.
2553-jeanne-d-arc-her-life-and-death:
Mrs. Oliphant wrote this life of Jeanne d'Arc for the Heroes of the Nations series, published in 1896 under the editorship of Evelyn Abbott. The Maid of Orleans rises from a peasant village to lead French armies, crown a king, and face trial and burning at Rouen.

Oliphant traces Jeanne's voices, her campaigns, her capture, and the trial that condemned her, with sympathy for her faith and courage. The book balances legend with record, and it reads as a clear, humane life of a girl who changed a war. It suits readers meeting Jeanne for the first time as well as those who know her story.
25656-the-mystery-of-a-turkish-bath:
Rita, the pen name of E. M. Gollan, writes this supernatural novel, one of some seventy novels under that name. The tale opens among women taking the waters at a grand seaside hotel in late Victorian England, a place doctors recommend for cures.

One day a strikingly beautiful woman joins them in the bath and charms the women already there. Another guest, Colonel Estcourt, knew her since childhood, when marriage between them seemed expected. Instead she went another way, and the bath, the hotel, and old love entwine into mystery.
25714-mother-hubbard-her-picture-book-co:
Walter Crane makes this picture book, Mother Hubbard's Picture Book, second in his picture book series, containing Mother Hubbard, The Three Bears, and The Absurd A.B.C., with original coloured pictures, an illustrated preface, and odds and end papers never before printed.

Mother Hubbard cranes her neck up the lane to see three bears pass. They go in, oddly, leading the Bodley, to buy an alphabet book. She draws nearer for a good look, and on her return finds he has run through her book. Crane's bright pictures carry nursery rhymes that generations of children know by heart.
25776-this-crowded-earth:
Robert Bloch writes this science fiction novel, This Crowded Earth, printed as a book-length novel complete in Amazing Stories for October 1958, with pictures by Finlay. Contents date chapters by person and year, from Harry Collins in 1997 and 1998 through President Winthrop in 1999.

Minnie Schultz in 2009, Michael Cavendish in 2027, Eric Donovan in 2031, and Jesse Pringle in 2039 follow, with Littlejohn in 2065 closing the run. A telescreen lights promptly at eight in the morning, and evils of long, dangerous years erupt in blood, as Bloch imagines a future Earth grown too crowded for its people.
26183-laurence-sterne-in-germany-a-contr:
Harvey Waterman Thayer's 1905 study, issued by Columbia University Press, traces Laurence Sterne's vogue in Germany from the sources. A note by Calvin Thomas calls it the first full attempt at the task, drawn from research in American and European libraries. Thayer follows Sterne's fame before and after The Sentimental Journey reached German readers.

Later chapters weigh Sterne's influence on German writers, his many imitators, and the backlash against him and his sentimental manner. A bibliography and index close the volume. The book serves students of English and German letters alike, showing how one English humourist helped shape a German literary age.
26366-the-electric-bath:
George M. Schweig's Electric Bath, issued by G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1877, treats the medical uses, effects, and appliance of galvanic and faradic baths. Schweig, a New York physician, built the book from an 1874 Medical Record article and letters of inquiry from doctors across America and Europe. He admits he groped in the dark, with no earlier experience to guide him.

He warns that the bath is no panacea, meeting many cases with negative or imperfect results, yet he seeks its merits on a basis of statistical truth. Special diseases follow, opening with rheumatism, frequent, painful, and often obstinate. Some advice rests on analogy with local electrical methods, not on his own trials. The book records early electrotherapy, hopes and limits alike.
2637-youth:
Leo Tolstoy wrote this autobiographical novel of youth, here translated by C. J. Hogarth, and it follows a young man finding a new view of life through friendship with Dimitri. The heart of that view is a conviction that moral improvement is easy, possible, and lasting.

Tolstoy traces his hero's efforts, failures, and fresh resolves, with the honesty that marks all his early work. University life, love, and faith each test the young man's ideals. The book reads as a frank record of growing up, and a first sketch of the moral seriousness that would fill Tolstoy's later masterpieces.
26623-the-brass-bell-or-the-chariot-of-d:
Eugène Sue wrote this tale of Caesar's Gallic invasion, translated from the French by Solon de Leon for the New York Labor News Company in 1907, with a new edition in 1916. Druids of Karnak and the Chief of the Hundred Valleys sound the call to arms. Tribes from Brittany gather before Vannes, near the bay of Morbihan, leaving fields, herds, and dwellings behind. Joel, his family, and his tribe march with them.

Albinik the mariner and his wife Meroë, dressed in sailor's garb, beard the lion in his den on a mission that may mean slavery, torture, or death. Chapters run from conflagration and trial to the battle of Vannes, master and slave, and sale into bondage. Sue turns conquest into a family saga of resistance, captivity, and Gallic pride.
26641-the-submarine-hunters-a-story-of-t:
Percy F. Westerman published this naval adventure with Blackie and Son at London, Glasgow, and Bombay in 1918, illustrated by E. S. Hodgson. It opens with Ross Trefusis and Vernon Haye, both about fifteen, whose sailing boat grounds off St. Mena's Island near Killigwent Hall on the North Cornish coast. Ross's father, Admiral Paul Trefusis, lives at the Hall, while Vernon's father serves with the Grand Fleet.

Kidnapping, a spell aboard U75, and a landing at Port Treherne follow, with a treacherous plot, smoke-signals, and H.M.S. Capella in the hunt. The boys go adrift in the Channel, face mines off the Belgian coast, and reach an affair off Kiel. The frontispiece shows the Black Cross flag lowered and raised again under the White Ensign, in a wartime boys' tale of patrol work.
26840-tin-foil-and-its-combinations-for-:
Henry L. Ambler, professor of operative dentistry at Western Reserve University, wrote this 1897 manual to give tin foil its due as a filling material. Tin had been used for teeth for more than a century, he notes, yet no single textbook had treated it fully enough for teacher and pupil alike. Nine chapters cover its history, its properties, and its combinations, in plain form meant to serve both classroom and clinic.

Ambler began using tin in 1867 after daily failures with amalgam fillings. For seven years he banished amalgam from his office in favor of tin, oxychloride, and gutta-percha. A survey of the University of Pennsylvania clinic for 1896–97 found gold in 55 per cent of fillings, tin in 15 per cent, and amalgam in 10 per cent. The book argues that tin deserved a larger share.
26903-determining-the-age-of-cattle-by-t:
George W. Pope of the Quarantine Division wrote this short bulletin for the Department of Agriculture, Farmers' Bulletin 1066, printed at Washington in August 1919. Its rule is simple: a beast's age can be judged from its second incisor teeth. Cattle carry eight incisors, all in the lower jaw. A calf shows two or more temporary teeth at birth, with all eight present in a month.

Near two years the center pair of temporary pinchers gives way to permanent pinchers, fully grown at two. First intermediates follow at two and a half to three, second intermediates at three and a half, and corner teeth at four and a half to five. Leveling and wear then mark the years. Pinchers level at six, middle pairs wear by nine, corners by ten. By twelve the arch runs nearly straight and the teeth stand as separated triangular stubs.
26908-conversations-on-chemistry-v-1-2-i:
A fifth edition, revised and enlarged, of this dialogue introduction to chemistry, printed for Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown at London in 1817. The author, herself a woman, explains that she learned chemistry not from crowded lecture demonstrations. Conversations with a friend and repeated experiments taught her instead, and she offers the book chiefly to the female sex. Three voices carry it: Mrs. B., the teacher, with her pupils Caroline and Emily.

Volume one treats simple bodies, from general principles, light and heat, and caloric through the chemical agencies of electricity to oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, sulphur, and phosphorus. The fifth edition adds the discoveries of the last four years, including gas-lights and the miner's lamp, while leaving doctrines unchanged. Old names in the text differ from modern terms, and a transcriber's note maps them: oxy-muriatic acid is chlorine, muriatic acid is hydrochloric acid.
27261-fantazius-mallare-a-mysterious-oat:
Ben Hecht's Fantazius Mallare, A Mysterious Oath, published by Covici-McGee in Chicago in 1922 with drawings by Wallace Smith, appeared in a limited edition of 2,025 numbered copies, this one number 832. Mallare, under a green-white street lamp, remembers a white throat and a pale, imploring face.

He has murdered her, yet she stands before him once more, and he smiles at his madness. Mallare desired to create for himself out of himself, to be God. His phantoms have grown so rich and strong that they confront him, in Hecht's fevered prose poem of guilt and illusion.
27327-agricultural-implements-and-machin:
John T. Schlebecker wrote this Smithsonian survey, number 17 in Smithsonian Studies in History and Technology, published by the Smithsonian Institution Press in Washington in 1972. It describes the agricultural implements and machines held by the National Museum of History and Technology, treating the objects as evidence for how American farming changed.

Readers move through tools and machines of the farm, set in their working context rather than shown as curiosities alone. The study follows the Smithsonian's aim of spreading knowledge through careful description of its own holdings. For students of farm history and technology, it is a solid museum-based reference.
27438-me-smith:
Caroline Lockhart published this western novel with Grosset and Dunlap in New York in February 1911, with illustrations by Gayle Hoskins, and it reached a seventh printing by August of that year. Its hero is Smith, called Me-Smith, and the chapters follow him across alkali hills, saddle-blanket swaps, and a great secret.

Smith makes medicine with the schoolmarm, Cupid wings a deputy sheriff, and a bug-hunter elucidates. Susie's Indian blood, the love medicine of the Sioux, and the murderer of White Antelope all enter the tangle. Mother love and savage passion conflict, as one chapter puts it. Lockhart writes frontier romance with humor and a sharp eye for character.
27529-the-peace-negotiations-between-the:
Rev. J. D. Kestell, secretary to the Orange Free State Government, and D. E. van Velden, secretary to the Government of the South African Republic, wrote this account of the peace negotiations. Van Velden translated and published it, with photos and facsimiles of original documents.

The negotiations ran between the two Boer governments and the representatives of the British Government. They ended in the peace concluded at Vereeniging on 31 May 1902. The book opens with a facsimile of Lord Kitchener's letter from Pretoria on 4 March 1902 to Mr. Schalk Burger. Portraits show the signatories for each republic. The account comes from the Boer side's own secretaries.
27561-the-boy-chums-in-the-forest-or-hun:
Wilmer M. Ely, author of The Boy Chums on Indian River and The Boy Chums in the Gulf of Mexico, published this boys' adventure with A. L. Burt in New York in 1910. It was copyrighted under the title The Young Plume Hunters, and its chums hunt plume birds in the Florida Everglades.

Chapters run from On the Way and Woodcraft through the 'Gator Hunters, the Quagmire, and the Battle, to the Bees and the Bear. Later come a flag of truce, a flight by night, capture, the swamp, and the Seminoles. The book opens at night in a wild Florida forest, with an owl hooting and a whip-poor-will calling. A frontispiece shows Charlie in the fork of a limb, saying they are in for it.
27872-a-history-of-the-french-novel-vol-:
George Saintsbury's History of the French Novel, volume two, covers the years 1800 to 1900 and was published by Macmillan in 1919. Saintsbury, late professor of rhetoric and English literature at Edinburgh, had corrected and added to volume one before issuing this sequel.

The volume surveys a century of French fiction from romanticism through realism and naturalism to the symbolists, judging novels as accomplished literature whatever their school. With its learning and strong opinions, it remains a classic English guide to Balzac, Flaubert, Zola, and their contemporaries. Saintsbury opens with addenda and corrigenda for volume one, answering a reviewer who thought him piqued.
28111-moment-of-truth:
Basil Wells's Moment of Truth is a short science-fiction tale about Ruth Halsey, a fourteen-year-old girl living on Mars. Ruth wakes in a bright room with false windows that look out on red dust, and dreams of home, friends, and dates. Her room, with its doll, mirror, and flowered walls, feels safe and known.

Slowly the wallpaper fades and shifts, and Ruth begins to doubt what is real around her. Wells, known for tales of the years near the War of 1812, here turns to a pioneer girl's adjustment to a strange new world. The story ends on a sharp question about memory, home, and what it means to belong.
28225-the-book-collector-a-general-surve:
W. Carew Hazlitt's The Book-Collector, London, 1904, surveys book collecting from the earliest times to his own day, at home and abroad. Hazlitt traces printed books and manuscripts, public and private libraries, and the founders and owners behind them, with notes on binding and on special copies. A key to a Sotheby's sale picture opens the volume.

Chapters follow Hazlitt's own career as a collector and writer, and tell anecdotes of dealers, auctions, and famous shelves. The book serves both new collectors, who learn terms and traps, and old hands, who enjoy its stories. It remains a classic guide to the pursuit of books.
28416-days-of-heaven-upon-earth:
A. B. Simpson's Days of Heaven Upon Earth, copyrighted in December 1897, is a year book of scripture texts and living truths for daily reading. Each day of the year, from January 1 through December 31, receives its own entry, so a reader can follow the book straight through the calendar.

Simpson, whose earlier volume pondered the words of Jesus, here offers short daily meditations meant to be read morning by morning through the year. The book belongs to devotional reading rather than to theology, and it gives modern readers a clear example of late Victorian evangelical piety in daily form.
28428-manual-of-surgery-volume-second-ex:
Alexis Thomson and Alexander Miles, both surgeons at the Edinburgh Royal Infirmary, wrote this second volume of their Manual of Surgery, revised and enlarged for its sixth edition in 1921. It covers surgery of the limbs, head, and neck, with 288 illustrations.

Chapters move from injuries of bones and joints through the shoulder, hip, knee, ankle, and foot, then to the scalp, skull, brain, spine, face, mouth, ear, nose, and neck. Each section describes injuries, diseases, and deformities in turn, making the book a working reference for students and practising surgeons of its day.
28491-dishes-beverages-of-the-old-south:
Martha McCulloch-Williams gathered the cooking of the Old South in Dishes & Beverages of the Old South, published by McBride, Nast of New York in October 1913. She writes from memory of Mammy's kitchen, where a biscuit block stood at the center of daily work. The book covers grace before meat, bread, bacon, hams, and drinks for thirsty souls.

Further chapters treat pies, puddings, Creole cookery, cakes, meats, poultry, game, eggs, soups, salads, and relishes. Vegetables, fruit desserts, sandwiches, pickles, preserves, coffee, tea, and chocolate follow, with notes on orchards, occasions, soap, and candles. It serves as both a cookbook and a record of Southern household life.
28608-inside-john-barth:
William W. Stuart's Inside John Barth, from Galaxy Magazine of June 1960, poses a strange bargain. Johnny Barth has money, success in several fields, fine company, and a life expectancy of 175 to 200 more years. He should be the happiest man alive, yet he is not, and he knows he is not crazy.

His secret is that he is not quite a man at all, but a colony, a settlement kept up like a locale. The tale rewinds ten years to a hunting trip after college, before a job in his Uncle John's dry-cleaning chain. Readers get a compact science-fiction joke with a serious edge about identity.
28694-young-alaskans-in-the-far-north:
Emerson Hough's Young Alaskans in the Far North, published by Harper and Brothers in 1918, sends three boys toward the midnight sun. Jesse Wilcox, fifteen and youngest, John Hardy, and Rob McIntyre gather at ragged Athabasca Landing, waiting for Uncle Dick. Rob, the quiet older boy they all look up to, watches the straggling settlement, its church spire, bank, stores, and Hudson's Bay post.

Chapters follow scows, the great brigade, grand rapids, white-water days, a steamboat, and a wild portage. The Mackenzie, the Arctic Circle, farthest north, the Rat Portage, Fort Yukon, the fur trade, and Dawson the golden city follow. Readers get a boys' northern journey, by river, portage, and midnight sun.
29070-brighter-britain-volume-1-of-2-or-:
William Delisle Hay wrote this 1882 book, Brighter Britain, or Settler and Maori in Northern New Zealand, volume one of two, published by Richard Bentley in London. Hay describes things as they are in the northern half of the North Island, home of the kauri pine, with some reference to past history. He insists he is not an emigration tout, a land salesman, or a tourist.

Hay went to New Zealand as an emigrant, meaning to spend his life as a colonist, and he writes from a settler's point of view. A Southey verse on the title page calls Britain to send her swarms abroad, since wherever her language lives, that land is English still. Readers get a settler's account of northern New Zealand in the 1880s, descriptive, personal, and frank about colonial life.
29159-acid-bath:
Vaseleos Garson wrote this science fiction story about Jon Karyl, the lone watcher on a small asteroid. Karyl, bolting a baffle plate onto a stationary rocket engine, misses the landing of a peculiar blue spaceship a few hundred yards from his plastic igloo. Six steel-blue creatures slide from its airlock and lope toward him.

The invaders, the Steel-Blues, have devised a weird twenty-one-day liquid test for their captive. Garson builds the horror from that premise: a solitary man, a strange bath, and three weeks of nerve-fraught waiting. Readers get a tense pulp tale of invasion and endurance, where the watcher becomes the watched and the test itself is the terror.
29210-out-of-the-north:
Howard V. Sutherland published this book of poems in New York in 1913, with a foreword by Joaquin Miller. Sutherland, author of Idylls of Greece and The Woman Who Could, writes here of the North: winter light, dark days, December, and the return of the sun. Klondike roses and a song for the return of birds bring the Yukon into lyric form.

Other poems honor Father Judge and follow two quests, a forest cotillion, and spruces of the forest. Miller's foreword frames the collection for readers. Readers get a slim volume of northern verse, where gold-rush country and the turning seasons supply the images, and where the cold itself becomes a kind of muse.
29292-the-old-game-a-retrospect-after-th:
Samuel G. Blythe published this book in New York in 1914, after three and a half years on the water-wagon, the slang for total abstinence from drink. Blythe, author of The Price of Place and Cutting It Out, writes as a man still early in his standing among those who have quit. In six years and six months more, he jokes, he will reach ten years.

Chapters look back from a hillock of abstinence, describe getting alcohol out of one's system, and answer the jeers of smart alecs. Blythe also counts what abstinence gives back: more time, leisure put to good uses, and freedom from alcohol's toll. Readers get a candid temperance memoir, personal and plainspoken, from the years before Prohibition.
29449-the-golden-fountain-or-the-soul-s-:
Lilian Staveley wrote this short book of faith in 1919, after years of seeking a close, felt sense of God rather than a mere assent to belief. Published in London by John M. Watkins, it speaks as one seeker to others, in plain, earnest prose. Its theme is the Pearl of Great Price: the deep prize that some seek by study, rite, or penance, and few claim to find.

Staveley argues that the search must turn inward, toward the heart, and that God is met by going where God is to be found, not by piling up proofs. Short chapters press the same point from fresh angles: longing, prayer, and the barrier that seems to block the way. Readers who care about prayer and the inner life will find a direct, tender guide.
29463-the-foreign-tour-of-messrs-brown-j:
Richard Doyle's comic book follows three English tourists, Brown, Jones, and Robinson, on a tour through Belgium, Germany, Switzerland, and Italy. The plain-text file holds only the captions to Doyle's drawings. Each line reads as a small joke or scene: a rough crossing to Ostend, a mail train to Dover, and natives who seize luggage and thrust cards into eager hands. The full charm lived in the pictures, but the captions still carry the fun.

Readers meet the classic Victorian tourist: bewildered, hurried, and keen to see it all. Doyle pokes gentle fun at travel, crowds, and the gap between grand sights and small mishaps. Those who love early comic art and travel humor will enjoy this brisk, picture-led jaunt across the Continent.
29572-whispering-smith:
Frank H. Spearman's 1906 novel, printed by Grosset and Dunlap with pictures by N. C. Wyeth and scenes from the Signal Film photo-play, opens with a wreck at Smoky Creek. News reaches Medicine Bend, sent from Point of Rocks, at five in the afternoon, while Sinclair himself oversees the making up of his wrecking train. Chapters follow the wrecking boss, Dicksie, George McCloud, and the crawling stone, through a final appeal and a misunderstanding.

Spearman writes a railroad western of loyalty, love, and hard duty on the line. Whispering Smith himself moves through the tale as a quiet, feared presence. Readers of western and railroad fiction will find a classic, well-plotted novel from the age when the train ruled the West.
29594-red-white-blue-socks-part-second-b:
Part second of the Sock Stories, the second book of the series by Aunt Fanny's Daughter, was printed in New York in 1863 by Leavitt and Allen. Its contents open with Colonel Freddy, or the march and encampment of the dashing volunteers, and a picture of Bull Run faces the text. A little lisping private cries that it is fun to be soldiers, and wishes the Southerners would come along.

The children play at war with buttons for insignia, in the earnest, patriotic spirit of the Civil War years. Their games mirror the real war their elders fight. Young readers and students of children's books will find a vivid, period volume where play and patriotism mix.
29689-henry-the-sixth:
M. R. James, provost of Eton, printed this Cambridge volume in 1919. It is a reprint of John Blacman's memoir of Henry VI, with a translation and notes. Blacman, a chaplain who knew the king, gathered tales of Henry's mild ways and good morals. He gave them the Latin title Collectarium Mansuetudinum. James gives the Latin text, an English rendering, and notes on the book itself.

Special notes treat a prayer to Henry in English verse, the manuscript tales of his miracles, and Blacman's own books. James also describes the small book's size, script, and woodcut of the crowned king. The volume suits readers who want a short, first-hand medieval life, set out with the care of a scholar.
29695-the-hound-from-the-north:
Ridgwell Cullum published this northern tale in 1904, with a frontispiece by Charles Livingston Bull. It opens under a pale sun low over mountain tops, with glaciers, pine woods, and the signs of a storm to come. Then it moves to a lonely ranch at Owl Hoot and the men who live by it. Mr. Zachary Smith, Leslie Grey, and the folk of the range cross paths over claims, debts, and old scores.

A hound runs through the tale, howling in the night and haunting the ranch, until the final chapters name it the avenger. Cullum mixes ranch work, blackmail, a stab in the dark, and an echo from the Alaskan mountains. The book is a brisk tale of the far north, where the land is hard and old wrongs do not rest.
30093-the-shepherd-of-the-north:
Richard Aumerle Maher sets a novel of northern ministry in snow country, where the Bishop of Alden practices his French on Arsene LaComb along a long Adirondack road. Arsene, from Three Rivers, cannot always follow the bishop's fine French. The bishop cannot always follow his, yet the pair make cheery companions through soft drifts and uncertain roads. They leave Lowville and the railroad behind in the purple dawn, heading into the hills.

Macmillan published the volume in March 1916, with reprints through February 1917. Its ten chapters trace a shepherd's work: the white horse chaplain, the choir unseen, the glow of dawn, the inner citadel, and the coming of the shepherd. Maher, author of The Heart of a Man, writes a warm, faith-centered tale of guidance, fear, and courage in a hard northern parish.
30304-psichopath:
Darrel T. Langart gives psi powers a hard test in a short tale from Analog, October 1960, with pictures by van Dongen. Clairvoyance and telepathy should make sabotage easy to solve, the tagline admits, at least at first thought. A man in a pastel blue topcoat walks with steady purpose through chill drizzle in Arlington, Virginia. His blue cap hood sits low, and a clear infrared face mask flips down against the icy wind.

No one notices him, an average man blending with others, his ordinary face seldom seen in public outside his own state. Beneath the calm walk, Senator John Peter Gonzales keeps a mental, fine-webbed, four-dimensional net around himself, feeling for the slightest touch of recognition. He wants no link to his destination, a six-floor brick building on a lower-middle-class street, on a visit that is not his first.
30639-border-breed-nor-birth:
Mack Reynolds writes Border, Breed nor Birth, part one of two, a science fiction story from Analog, July 1962, illustrated by Schoenherr. Its tagline quotes Kipling: border, breed, and birth did not matter when two strong men met face to face, then asks whether they count when two strong ideologies meet.

El Hassan, who aims to rule all North Africa, commands a tiny band of six, among them a slight twenty-four-year-old girl. He faces a global alliance: the Reunited Nations, the French Community, Common Europe, the Soviet Complex, and the United States of the Americas beside it. Reynolds turns ideology, tyranny, and resistance into a tense future tale.
31256-how-the-black-st-domingo-legion-sa:
T. G. Steward's 1899 paper, number five in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, retells the siege of Savannah in 1779 and the part played by the Black St. Domingo Legion. Steward opens by quoting a brief schoolbook account in which D'Estaing joins Lincoln, an assault fails with a thousand lives lost, Pulaski is mortally wounded, and Sergeant Jasper dies grasping his banner.

Against that thin version, Steward argues the attack was well planned and failed only because British regulars defended the works with skill. He traces how the Black legion's stand saved the retreating patriot army. The paper is an early work of Black military history, reclaiming a role textbooks had let fade.
31265-aunt-hannah-and-seth:
James Otis's 1900 children's story, published by Thomas Y. Crowell in New York, follows Seth Barrows, called Limpy Seth for his uneven legs, and his tiny white dog Snip. It opens on a June morning near the New York approach to the Brooklyn Bridge, where Seth, small boy with dog in arms, hesitates before the living tide of traffic. Meanwhile a shrill-voiced red-haired friend forces a passage to join him.

Six chapters carry the pair from an advertisement and the country to Aunt Hannah herself, a flight, an accident, and sunshine. Warm, old-fashioned, and full of city and country incident, the book is a gentle tale of a boy, his dog, and the people who take them in.
3130-captain-john-smith:
Warner meant this book as a familiar, light life of Captain John Smith. It was planned for a series on American notables, written without historic gravity. Study soon made the job more serious than he expected. Smith invites jokes, but real puzzles cling to his career. Warner chose to state the truth and strip away the fables around the adventurer.

Earlier lives mostly paraphrased Smith's own account and took his estimate of himself. Newer research let Warner test that story against other evidence. The result keeps Smith's color while refusing his word on everything. That harder record is the book's gift: Smith cut down to human size, without losing his color.
31330-modern-industrialism-and-the-negro:
Archibald H. Grimké's 1908 paper, number twelve in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, asks what modern industrialism will do with Black Americans. Passing into its huge hopper and between its millstones, Grimké wonders one thing. Would Black Americans emerge as grain the nation could use, or as husks doomed, as the Indian was, to extinction amid racial and industrial rivalry?

He turns to the founders, who reared the republic on human equality and inalienable rights. Yet they made an exception at the threshold for African slavery as an industrial system, the exception on which the dark drama of national history turns. The paper reads that past, written word by word in social evolution, to guess the fateful answer still being written.
31354-death:
Maurice Maeterlinck's Death, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1912, is a philosophical essay on mortality. Maeterlinck was the Belgian writer known for The Life of the Bee and The Treasure of the Humble. He turns here to the question every reader must face: what death is, and how the living should think about it. The essay is reflective rather than doctrinal, and it speaks in the plain, searching voice of his essays.

Readers will find Maeterlinck weighing fear, mystery, and consolation without offering easy answers. The book's lasting interest lies in its tone: calm, humane, and willing to sit with uncertainty. For those reading Maeterlinck as a thinker rather than a playwright, Death shows his philosophy at its most personal, asking how knowledge of death should change the way we live.
31385-notes-on-the-diplomatic-history-of:
Lucien Wolf's Notes on the Diplomatic History of the Jewish Question was published by the Jewish Historical Society of England in 1919. It presents the subject with texts of protocols, treaty stipulations, and other public acts and official documents. Wolf wrote from the Mocatta Library and Museum at University College, London. He traces how the Jewish question entered European diplomacy, from congresses and treaties to the pledges states made and broke.

The book's strength is its documents: readers can read the actual texts behind the narrative, not summaries alone. Wolf treats a long, painful history with scholarly care, showing how Jewish rights became a matter of international law and politics. For students of modern Jewish history and diplomacy, it remains a source-rich study, grounded in the archive rather than in polemic.
31462-oliver-goldsmith:
E. S. Lang Buckland's Oliver Goldsmith was published in London by George Bell and Sons in 1909 as part of Bell's Miniature Series of Great Writers. It is a short life of the Irish writer. Its contents move from "The Best Beloved of English Writers" through "The Deserted Village" and "The Traveller" to London. They continue through "The Citizen of the World," the Literary Club, debts and dignities, consummate comedy, and the poet and essayist. A list of Goldsmith's works closes the volume.

Buckland treats Goldsmith's life through his writings, showing how the poems, essays, and plays grew from experience. The portrait that opens the book, from a painting by Reynolds, suits a writer beloved for warmth and humor. Readers seeking a compact introduction to Goldsmith will find this little biography a good starting point, with his chief works placed in the order of his life.
31478-rollo-in-society-a-guide-for-youth:
George S. Chappell's Rollo in Society, a guide for youth, was published by G. P. Putnam's Sons in a new edition revised by the author in 1922, with cuts by Wm. Hogarth Jr. A notice to parents explains the book's double aim. It is meant first to entertain youthful readers. The notice also hopes parents will use it as a companion for guiding children through childhood's difficulties. Rollo himself, pictured in the front matter, is the cheerful pupil of this social schooling.

Chappell treats manners as an adventure, with humor rather than scolding. The book's satirical edge comes from treating children's social blunders as seriously as adult ones. Readers today will find a period piece on American manners, funny in its formality, and a reminder that every generation worries, in its own way, about how children should behave.
31547-youth:
Isaac Asimov's short story Youth opens with Red and Slim finding two odd little creatures the morning after hearing thunder. The boys know their new pets could never be shown to their parents. Red, whose real name is not Red, and Slim, named for his slight figure by his new friend, become friends at once. Theirs is the swift, unquestioning friendship of children not yet adolescent.

The story follows the boys and their secret pets through a country summer, with an adult world hovering just beyond their game. Asimov, already a master of the short science-fiction tale, builds the story toward a surprise that reframes everything the boys have seen. Readers will find a brief, clever story about childhood, curiosity, and the strangeness hiding in an ordinary field.
31597-out-of-the-earth:
George Edrich's story of a lost people opens with a headnote that calls it a tale of a near-future people forgotten by history. Offences against the State mean elimination in the Black Passage, which is death, and the little group at the story's heart is to die. They walk through blackness, with only two lamps kept lighted to frighten away the Groles.

The narrator's diary begins on First Awake, 2 Juli, 2207, with Last City far behind and Nina sleeping close beside him. The State Guards in black uniforms came for them in the sleep hours, and the group now presses on, determined to prove that death is a myth. Edrich's tale joins flight, faith, and a forgotten past.
31674-comments-on-the-taxonomic-status-o:
J. Knox Jones Jr.'s paper on the taxonomic status of Apodemus peninsulae, with description of a new subspecies from North China, appeared as volume nine, number eight, of the University of Kansas Publications. It runs pages 337 to 346, with one figure and one table, and is dated August 15, 1956. It weighs where the field mouse Apodemus peninsulae belongs in classification.

Jones then describes a new subspecies from North China, setting out the characters that mark it off from its relatives. The paper is a compact piece of mammal taxonomy, built on specimens and measurements, and it gives the new form its formal place in the published record.
31840-ring-once-for-death:
Robert Arthur's short story Ring Once for Death was printed in Amazing Stories in March 1954. It follows Mark and Edith Williams, a modern twentieth-century couple for whom the power of the old gods seems nothing to worry about. Its headnote adds, after all, everybody dies.

The couple returns to Sam Kee's little shop on Mott Street, unchanged in twenty years. Its dusty jars hold ginseng root and tigers' whiskers, little bronze Buddhas, and fine jade. They are there to buy a twentieth-anniversary present, perhaps a bell. Readers get a supernatural tale in which an old shop, a bell, and old gods prove more dangerous than a modern couple expects.
31900-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris's volume thirteen of Historical Tales, the Romance of Reality, published by J. B. Lippincott Company, tells the story of King Arthur. Its first chapter, The Magic Sword, opens in that far-off era of chivalry and knight-errantry. Wandering knights sought adventures far and wide, and every damsel in distress found a valiant champion.

Arthur, flower of chivalry and founder of the famed Round Table order, follows Uther Pendragon. After Uther's death anarchy prevailed, until Merlin, master of all mysteries, shaped the destiny of the land. Readers get Arthurian legend retold for young readers, from the ancient legends and chronicles of chivalry.
31972-my-service-in-the-u-s-colored-cava:
Frederick W. Browne's paper My Service in the U.S. Colored Cavalry was read before the Ohio Commandery of the Loyal Legion on March 4, 1908. It tells how a sergeant of over two years in a hard-fighting infantry regiment took a commission in the 1st U.S. Colored Cavalry. Browne, second lieutenant of that regiment, was encamped at Newport News, Virginia, when Major John G. Chambers asked if he would like a commission in the new regiment forming at Fort Monroe.

Within two or three days Browne received orders mustering him out and reporting to Colonel Garrard for duty. Early the next morning he showed the sentry at the wharf his mustering-out order as authority for leaving. Readers get a veteran's first-hand account of service with Black cavalrymen in the Civil War.
31977-the-fourth-massachusetts-cavalry-i:
Major Edward T. Bouvé's account of the Fourth Massachusetts Cavalry in the closing scenes of the war for the maintenance of the Union, from Richmond to Appomattox, centers on the battle at High Bridge. Its frontispiece shows Colonel Arnold A. Rand of the Fourth Massachusetts Volunteer Cavalry.

Bouvé opens with the long history of American cavalry. He notes laws for a mounted force passed in 1648, when Massachusetts Bay was not yet of age. By 1675 there were five troops of cavalry in the war with Metacomet, or King Philip. Readers get a regimental history that sets a Civil War cavalry unit in a tradition stretching back to colonial Massachusetts.
32052-grenfell-knight-errant-of-the-nort:
Fullerton Waldo's 1924 book Grenfell: Knight-Errant of the North, published in Philadelphia by George W. Jacobs and Company, is a life of Wilfred Grenfell, the medical missionary of Labrador, by the author of With Grenfell on the Labrador and Down the Mackenzie. Waldo dedicates the volume to Mary Castleman Davis, and opens with a letter from Grenfell dated December 15, 1923.

Grenfell tells Waldo that he, who has sampled the salt breezes of the North aboard Grenfell's boat, has imbibed the spirit behind a belief. That belief is that in a world like ours we can all be knights. Readers get a warm, first-hand biography of the Labrador doctor, his boats, his hospitals, and his northern people.
32058-american-slave-trade-or-an-account:
Jesse Torrey, Junior, a physician, published this exposé in Philadelphia in 1817, reprinted in London in 1822 with five plates. Its full title states its charge. Slave dealers took free people from some states, carried them away, and sold them as slaves in other states, practising horrible cruelties in the traffic. Torrey adds reflections on the project of forming a colony of American Blacks in Africa, with documents on that project.

The preface opens with a text from Exodus: he that steals a man and sells him, or if he be found in his hand, shall surely be put to death. Torrey numbers his paragraphs throughout, a practice he notes as useful for reference. Readers get a rare, early American abolitionist document, written by a witness to a domestic trade in free Black people, and aimed at readers who might otherwise look away from it.
32103-elsie-in-the-south:
Martha Finley's Elsie in the South, published by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1899, belongs to her long-running Elsie books. The story opens on a December morning, as Lucilla Raymond lies listening to rain and sleet dash against her bedroom windows. She sighs that there will be no early stroll about the grounds with papa that day, then checks herself, trusting that all changes of season are appointed for the best.

From that domestic opening, the book settles into the pleasures of a Southern home: warm rooms, a kind father, and sisters in adjoining bedrooms, with Lucilla careful not to wake Grace. Finley's tone is gentle and pious, with family affection and faith shaping everyday choices. Readers get a period family story for young readers, where storms keep everyone indoors and home itself, with its routines and its loved ones, provides the adventure.
32286-a-letter-to-lord-robert-bertie-rel:
A Letter to Lord Robert Bertie, relating to his conduct in the Mediterranean and his defence of Admiral Byng, was printed in London for R. Griffiths in Paternoster Row in 1757, priced at one shilling, with a Horace epigraph. Its opening addresses Bertie directly: characters like yours, it says, are regarded with impartial attention by human society, and the world impatiently expects conduct suitable to rank and dignity.

Those entrusted with the charter of liberties or the revenge of wrongs, the letter argues, lie under the strongest obligations honour or gratitude can impose. They must guard their nation's rights and carry out its anger. If they fail to strive their utmost, the people, fretful at their losses, will not forbear reflecting on the supposed authors of those losses. Readers get an eighteenth-century political pamphlet, sharp, formal, and aimed at a lord's Mediterranean conduct.
32292-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris's Historical Tales: The Romance of Reality, volume fourteen, King Arthur, was published by J. B. Lippincott Company in Philadelphia and London. Its copyrights date from 1891, 1904, and 1908, and it retells Arthurian legend as history. Morris, author of Half-Hours with the Best American Authors and Tales from the Dramatists, presents the volume as part of a fifteen-volume elite edition. Conway Castle serves as frontispiece.

Its eighth book, Tristram and Isolde at Joyous Gard, runs from The Treachery of King Mark and How Tristram Befooled Dinadan through the road to Lonazep and Palamides at the Red City. It continues to the tournament at Lonazep, its second day, the woes of two lovers, and the rivalry of Tristram and Palamides. Readers get a Victorian retelling of the Tristram legend, where treachery, tournaments, and doomed love carry the Arthurian romance.
32476-the-twelve-months-of-the-year-with:
The Twelve Months of the Year, published in Portland by Bailey and Noyes with a picture for each month, teaches children the calendar in northern latitudes. It opens by asking how many months there are. It then recites the old verse on thirty days in September, April, June, and November, twenty-eight in February, and thirty-one in the rest, with twenty-nine in leap year. Each month then gets its own picture and short lesson.

January brings cold, bare trees, frozen ground, and snow, with advice to bring wood and make a good fire. February stays cold but lengthens, as crocuses and snowdrops appear, a sign the book links to children turning from naughtiness to goodness. The volume suits very young readers learning seasons, weather, and the rhythm of the year.
32618-monsoons-of-death:
Gerald Vance sends Lieutenant Ward Harrison, fresh from commission, to a Mars observation station as a meteorologist. His task is plain survey work on air and weather, the unglamorous base for all later travel, settlement, and use of raw materials.

At the station Harrison finds his predecessor Halliday, a man so ruled by fear that three years of work remain undone.
