When monsoon storms bring rasping creatures against the walls, Harrison must fight beside the very man he scorned, and learn whether courage or terror will rule the night. The station itself feels like a trap. Walls, storms, and fear press in on both men alike.
32641-earthsmith:
Milton Lesser tells of Smith, a twenty-seven-year-old from Earth who joins the Interstellar Space School. At registration a machine asks his planet and age, and the crowd laughs when Earth means nothing to them. A small green-haired man dubs him Earthsmith, and the name sticks.

Smith faces scorn in class and on the Wortan mat, where brute strength rules and mind powers are banned. Yet he answers his mockers with a proud speech for Earth, a world he calls ages ahead of theirs in culture. The tale turns on whether a stranger can earn respect where no one knows his home.
32663-ye-of-little-faith:
Rog Phillips opens with a startling vanishing: John Henderson, a mathematics professor, disappears mid-lecture before forty-three students, leaving only a watch and a belt buckle on the floor. Police search his hotel room and trace his bank book, but find no motive.

As more people vanish, a young man who knew Henderson's ideas starts to test a strange theory, that belief itself may open a door to another system of things. The tale asks whether faith, doubt, and the mind's hidden depths can move a body from one world to another.
32667-the-holes-and-john-smith:
Edward W. Ludwig tells of Jimmie Stanley and his combo at the Space Room in Marsport, on the Grand Canal. Bass man Ziggy has cut two fingers on a can of Saturnian ice-fish, and boss Ke-teeli, eight feet three of Martian scorn, threatens their jobs. A replacement must play, or there will be no music.

Into the gap steps John Smith, a ragged little man from a hole, whose music is straight from heaven. For three golden days the cash register rings without pause. Yet John has lost his own time dimension, and if he cannot prove his theory and return, his name will stand disgraced.
32671-the-doors-of-death:
Arthur B. Waltermire tells of Judson McMasters, a rich banker lying sick in his great house, watched by his faithful servant Biggs. Drugs, fever, and a small portrait of Napoleon fill the sickroom, while Biggs keeps curtains drawn and fears for his master.

McMasters dreads one fate above all: his father and grandfather died of the family malady, and his grandfather was buried alive. He asks Biggs plainly whether men truly die, and faces his end with grim candor. The tale turns on that fear, and on what waits behind the doors its title names.
32743-the-silver-cross-or-the-carpenter-:
Eugene Sue tells this episode from his Mysteries of the People, translated from the French and published in New York by the International Publishing Company in 1899. The preface holds the story up as a mirror to the capitalist class, its orators, pulpiteers, politicians, and lawyers.

Genevieve, a slave of Aurelia, wife of a Roman named Gremion in Marseilles, sails with her mistress and master for Judea in the fifteenth year of the Emperor Tiberius. There she witnesses the Carpenter of Nazareth, his parables such as the lost sheep, and his trial before Caiaphas. Sue frames an ancient struggle of oppressors and toilers as a warning for modern times.
32827-think-yourself-to-death:
C. H. Thames sends Johnny Mayhem to Ophiuchus IX in the borrowed body of an elderly Sirian gentleman, in a story from Amazing Stories of March 1957. The Sirian's pince-nez, charcoal jumper, and black string-tie draw laughs in streets where men wear only loin cloths. Mayhem, who wears bodies the way other people wear clothes, ignores them with borrowed dignity.

The Galactic Observer, Kovandaswamy of Bombay, explains that Ophiuchus IX is one of the Forgotten Worlds, colonized from India in the first great outflux from Earth. Isolated for generations behind a dust cloud, it is only now being found again. Denebian Export hires local jet pilots, including Pandit Gandhi Menon and Sria Krishna, to fly to the Empty Places. The title's threat hangs over a world where thought itself may prove lethal.
32905-mask-of-death:
Paul Ernst's weird tale, from Weird Tales in August-September 1936, is set in Blue Bay, a Maine summer resort built from scratch on a fine bay. Millionaires poured eighteen million dollars into its homes, beaches, hotels, waterworks, and landing field, and on its formal opening night every light blazes. Behind that bright, model town waits a strange criminal who calls himself Doctor Satan.

The tale's dread grows from a paralysis that strikes without warning, the terrible doom with which Doctor Satan punishes his foes. Ernst builds his horror slowly, letting the resort's perfection curdle into fear. It is a pulp story of its period, mixing a modern planned town with an old-fashioned villain, and it rewards readers who enjoy menace served with a straight face.
33178-the-holy-earth:
L. H. Bailey's Holy Earth argues that the earth itself is good, kindly, and holy, and that farming must be judged by that standard. It was published in New York in 1916 with a copyright of 1915. Bailey divides the book into a statement that the earth is good and holy, and consequences, from the habit of destruction through the farmer's relation to the subdividing of land.

Later chapters treat a new map, a public program, an honest day's work, spiritual contact with nature, and the struggle for existence in war. They go on to daily fare, admiration of good materials, and keeping the beautiful earth. Bailey, a leading American horticulturist, writes for farmers and citizens alike, urging care for soil as a moral duty. The book remains a founding text of agrarian thought, and a quiet, earnest call to treat land as a trust.
33259-the-day-of-his-youth:
Alice Brown's novel opens with the death of Francis Hume's mother at his birth, a loss that shapes his whole youth. His father, a man of honored name, bears the blow with grief that ripples far past the family circle. The boy grows up under the shadow of a tragedy he never knew first-hand. Brown traces how that early loss colors Francis's ties, hopes, and choices as he comes of age.

First printed in 1897, the book is a quiet study of character rather than a tale of high adventure. Brown writes with care for inner life, letting small scenes and talks reveal what her people feel and hide. Readers who enjoy a thoughtful novel of family, duty, and growth will find here a tender, well-wrought story of a young man finding his way.
33268-maria-edgeworth:
Helen Zimmern's life of Maria Edgeworth, in the Famous Women series, traces the Irish novelist's career and character. Copyrighted in 1883, it notes that no full life of Edgeworth had yet appeared in America, and draws on notices and papers then at hand. Zimmern follows Edgeworth from her family circle to her fame as a writer of tales about Irish life, education, and society.

The book is short and readable, made for general readers rather than scholars alone. It places Edgeworth among her peers, from George Eliot to George Sand, and shows why her work mattered to readers of her day. For those new to Edgeworth, it is a clear first portrait of a witty, observant author who shaped the novel of manners.
33448-saint-bonaventure-the-seraphic-doc:
Laurence Costelloe's Saint Bonaventure, the Seraphic Doctor and Minister General of the Franciscans, tells the life of the great medieval friar. Published in the Friar Saints series, edited for Franciscan lives by Osmund and C. M. Antony, the book carries the church's nihil obstat and imprimatur. Costelloe, a Franciscan father, writes with devotion and learning.

The life suits readers of saints and medieval history, offering a clear account of Bonaventure's thought, rule, and holiness. Its tone is reverent and scholarly, aimed at Catholics and students alike. For those who love the Franciscan story, it is a solid, well-sourced portrait of a doctor of the church, seraphic in name and deed.
33477-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This appendix volume of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the work's own history. It runs from its first edition in three volumes, 1768 to 1771, through ten editions to the eleventh, published in twenty-nine volumes in 1910 and 1911. Its pages list the growth of the great reference work, edition by edition, showing how a Scottish venture became a world authority.

The volume suits readers of publishing history, offering a concise, factual record of the Britannica's making. Its tone is scholarly and plain, with dates and volumes set out in order. For students of reference works, it is a useful guide to how knowledge was gathered, revised, and sold across two centuries.
33568-history-of-the-war-between-mexico-:
Brantz Mayer, formerly secretary of the United States legation in Mexico, wrote this history of the war between Mexico and the United States. Mayer opens by calling the war, which broke out in the spring of 1846, an event of great importance, breaking a long peace among Christian nations since the fall of Napoleon. Illustrations show Santa Anna and the battles of Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma.

The first volume begins with Mexico's people and government and the causes that led to fighting, before moving into the campaigns themselves. Mayer writes as a diplomat-historian with first-hand knowledge of Mexico, aiming to explain the conflict to American readers while it was still fresh. The history remains a valuable contemporary account of the war's origins and early course.
33756-village-life-in-america-1852-1872-:
Caroline Cowles Richards tells village life in America from 1852 to 1872, including the Civil War, as recorded in the diary of a schoolgirl. The new and enlarged edition of 1913, with an introduction by Margaret E. Sangster, follows Richards from family notes, a famous school, girls, and hoop skirts through runaways, Bible study, and essays. It continues through lake picnics, a pyramid of beauty, preachers, votes for women, fires, sleighing, and prayer.

Later years bring truants and pickles, tableaux and charades, a spiritual seance, gymnastics, Lincoln's inauguration, Civil War school enthusiasm, and lectures. Dedicated to her brothers James and John and her sister Anna, the diary preserves small-town New York life in a young voice. Historians and general readers alike will enjoy its immediacy and its window onto ordinary American girlhood in a turbulent era.
33776-william-bradford-of-plymouth:
Albert H. Plumb wrote this short life of William Bradford, published in Boston in 1920. Bradford was a boy in Austerfield, England, who became a Pilgrim and later governor of Plymouth Colony. Plumb tells the story in five parts, from boyhood and the voyage to his early duties, later rule, and last acts.

The book stresses Bradford as a plain, steady leader who put the colony's good ahead of his own pride. It draws on his own record of Plymouth and on the work of later writers about New England. Readers gain a clear, brief account of how one man helped hold a small colony together.
33876-the-wave-an-egyptian-aftermath:
Algernon Blackwood published this novel in London in 1916, dedicating it to Egypt's forgetful and unwilling child. Its hero has been haunted since childhood by a wave of odd, tawny color that rises behind him, curls to fall, and then hangs still. It threatens but never falls, and the pause torments him.

Blackwood ties the wave to Egypt, to memory, and to a fate that waits for its right moment. The novel moves between dream and waking life, dread and release. It remains a strange, atmospheric tale of a mind shaped by one image it cannot shake.
33991-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Volume four of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica runs from Bisharin to Calgary, published in New York in 1910 as part of a twenty-nine-volume set issued in 1910 and 1911. The edition followed ten earlier editions reaching back to three volumes in 1768 to 1771, and it was copyrighted by the University of Cambridge.

A list of initials opens the volume, matching each signed article to its writer, from keepers of museum departments to university scholars. Readers find here the reference work at its early twentieth-century height. The volume serves as a solid source for the arts, sciences, and general knowledge of its day.
34136-pip-a-romance-of-youth:
Ian Hay's 1917 novel Pip follows a boy from childhood to manhood in three books. Book one shows Pip and his sister Pipette in nursery scrapes and at Mr. Pocklington's school, with the first signs of his vocation.

Book two brings a cricket week and life at first hand, while book three closes the road with an old game and a Latin tag about nature returning. Hay writes with schoolboy humour and warmth, tracing how a willing, wayward lad grows into a man. Hay sets the three books under tags from the ages of man, from infant to journey's end.
3545-the-complete-poetical-works-of-oliv:
Austin Dobson edits the complete poems of Oliver Goldsmith in this Oxford edition, with an introduction and notes. Dobson explains that the volume reprints and extends his earlier Selected Poems of 1887, adding the whole of Goldsmith's poetry with fresh notes and illustrations. Contents include The Traveller, The Deserted Village, The Hermit, An Elegy on the Death of a Mad Dog, and songs such as When Lovely Woman Stoops to Folly.

Goldsmith's verse mixes gentle satire, rural feeling, and clear, musical lines. The edition suits readers who want Goldsmith the poet rather than the novelist of The Vicar of Wakefield, with notes that explain old references. It remains a handy single volume for students and lovers of eighteenth century poetry.
3748-a-journey-into-the-interior-of-the-:
Jules Verne sends a German professor, his nephew, and their Icelandic guide Hans down into the earth in this classic adventure tale. A runic manuscript points to a crater in Iceland, and the shadow of Mount Scartaris at noon marks the middle chimney as the way in. The party climbs down past lava tubes and rock walls, then finds an underground sea, strange light, and creatures from ages long past.

Frederick Amadeus Malleson's 1877 translation keeps the science lectures and the jokes in balance, with the professor shouting for the center of the globe while Hans answers with a calm forward. The book moves from Hamburg study to volcanic descent without pause. Readers who like voyages of wonder will find here the pattern for a hundred later tales of lost worlds below.
4227-tom-swift-and-his-wireless-message-:
A Tom Swift adventure follows the young inventor and his wireless message to castaways on Earthquake Island. In a chapter on vol-planing to earth, Mr. Damon announces his company, and Tom warns that his Butterfly monoplane is not like the Red Cloud airship.

Riding the monoplane holds more danger than riding the airship, since engine failure leaves a flyer gliding down. Tom, his father, and Damon face the flight with boyish courage and mechanical know-how. Young readers who enjoy invention tales will find a brisk, old-fashioned adventure.
4275-ruth:
Elizabeth Gaskell published Ruth in book form with Chapman and Hall in 1853. It follows Ruth, a dressmaker's apprentice, from her workroom and a visit to the Shire-Hall. She passes through perilous places and a stay in North Wales. Troubles gather about her, and a crisis forces hard choices.

Later chapters bring Ruth into the household of the dissenting minister Thurstan Benson and his sister Faith. After five years, she serves as a governess in the Bradshaw family. There recognition, a forged deed, and a meeting on the sands test her past against her new life. Gaskell treats a young woman's fall and her effort to live honestly afterward with sympathy.
4276-north-and-south:
Elizabeth Gaskell's North and South opens in a London drawing room. Margaret Hale watches her cousin Edith, lovely in white muslin and blue ribbons. Edith prepares for marriage to Captain Lennox and a new life at Corfu. Margaret, who grew up beside Edith, feels the loss of her companion.

Wedding dresses and ceremonies fill the house as the parting nears. From that southern opening the novel moves Margaret north to a mill town. There she meets manufacturers, workers, and a different code of life. Gaskell sets the manners of the south against the industry of the north, and Margaret learns to judge both worlds more fairly.
4379-the-fortunate-youth:
William J. Locke wrote this novel around Paul Kegworthy, who lived with his mother, his stepfather Mr. Button, and six little Buttons in a grimy house in a northern manufacturing town. The home held two rooms plus a scullery, in a street of identical grimy houses. Mr. and Mrs. Button both held factory jobs and let rooms to single working men.

Paul, the fortunate youth of the title, rises from that unpromising start toward a larger life. Locke follows his luck, his loves, and his climb with humor and sympathy. The novel is a rags-to-consideration story, told without sentimentality, about a boy who makes his fortune by wit, charm, and hard work.
4499-complete-short-works-of-george-mere:
George Meredith's entire short works are gathered here, from Farina and the Case of General Ople to the Tale of Chloe and the House on the Beach. The Gentleman of Fifty and the unfinished comedy The Sentimentalists follow, with miscellaneous prose closing the volume. Farina opens the set in lusty ages when Kaisers drank green-eyed wine at Aachen.

The collection shows Meredith outside his great novels: in romance, comedy, and essay, with his wit in smaller compass. Readers can sample his range in an evening, from Rhineland legend to London courtship. The volume suits those who know the novels and want the shorter pieces that surround them.
4500-complete-project-gutenberg-works-of:
George Meredith's collected works in this volume start with his early Arabian entertainment, The Shaving of Shagpat. They run on through the great Victorian novels that made his name. Readers will find The Ordeal of Richard Feverel, Sandra Belloni, Rhoda Fleming, Evan Harrington, Vittoria, Harry Richmond, Beauchamp's Career, The Egoist, The Tragic Comedians, and Diana of the Crossways.

Later novels such as One of Our Conquerors, Lord Ormont and His Aminta, and The Amazing Marriage sit beside shorter fiction. Essays on comedy, miscellaneous prose, war letters, and three volumes of poems round out the set. Taken together, the set lets a reader trace Meredith from fanciful romance to sharp social comedy. It is a library in one file, best dipped into novel by novel rather than read straight through.
4523-on-conducting-u-eber-das-dirigiren-:
Richard Wagner wrote this treatise on the art of conducting, translated here by Edward Dannreuther, to argue that a conductor does far more than beat time. Wagner draws on his own work in the opera house and concert hall, and on the playing he heard from leading orchestras of his day. His subject is style: how a conductor shapes tempo, phrasing, and balance so that a score sounds as its composer meant it to sound.

Wagner attacks routine, hurry, and empty display, and he praises conductors who study the music, feel its pulse, and lead players without fuss. Singers, players, and listeners all come into his argument, since bad conducting spoils even fine music. Readers get a sharp, opinionated guide to a craft that is often unseen, and a window into how nineteenth-century music was actually performed.
4528-the-heart-s-highway-a-romance-of-vi:
Mary E. Wilkins sets this romance in Virginia in 1682, in the colony around Jamestown. The narrator, a man of thirty, rides to meeting one April Sunday with Mary Cavendish, just eighteen, while her grandmother and elder sister stay home. Madam Judith Cavendish, past seventy yet still riding like a young woman, stands for the tough older generation that built these swampy estates.

From that ride grows a story of love, family pride, and colonial manners, with enslaved workers, great houses, and churchgoing society in the background. Wilkins writes the past in careful, old-fashioned detail, and she lets her heroine's choices carry the plot. Readers get a gentle historical romance about courtship and duty in early Virginia, told by a man looking back on his youth.
4557-the-idea-of-progress-an-inquiry-int:
J. B. Bury, Regius Professor of Modern History at Cambridge, wrote this inquiry into the idea of progress, dedicating it to Saint-Pierre, Condorcet, Comte, Spencer, and other optimists named in the volume. His preface says we may believe in progress or not, but we should still examine where the idea came from. For Bury, earthly progress has become the general test by which social aims and theories are judged, good or bad.

Chapters trace the idea through Bodin, Bacon, and Cartesian thought. They go on to degeneration, Fontenelle, Saint-Pierre, Montesquieu, Voltaire, the encyclopaedists, economists, and Rousseau. Readers get a clear history of an idea, not a sermon for or against it. It is a useful guide to how the modern West came to expect tomorrow to be better than today.
4664-light-life-and-love-selections-from:
W. R. Inge gathered Light, Life, and Love in 1919, as selections from the German mystics of the Middle Ages, in a second edition. Its contents run from an introduction through Eckhart and Tauler, to meditations on the seven words from the cross, Suso, Ruysbroek, and the Theologia Germanica. Inge presents these writers as the heart of a movement English readers often know only through a later, softer book.

Most English readers, he says, take the Imitation of Christ as the representative of medieval German mysticism. In reality Thomas a Kempis was only a semi-mystic, who tones down Eckhart, the great original thinker of the school. To find German mysticism at its strongest, Inge argues, we must go back a full hundred years. Readers get a scholarly doorway into Eckhart and his heirs, with selections chosen for depth and clarity.
4669-town-and-country-or-life-at-home-an:
John S. Adams published Town and Country, or Life at Home and Abroad, Within and Without Us, at Boston in 1855. Its contents mix short poems and sketches. Titles include Saved by Kindness, The Love of Elinore, The Old Tree and Its Lesson, Voices from the Spirit Land, The Beacon Light, and Bear Up. A welcome song to spring, the hope of the fallen, and thoughts that come from long ago follow.

Later pieces include Determined to Be Rich, Forget Me Not, and What Is Truth. They go on to The Homestead Visit, The Mariner's Song, Light in Darkness, Mount Vernon and the Tomb of Washington, and Freedom's Gathering Song. Adams writes for home reading, with moral feeling and patriotic warmth. Readers get a mid-century American miscellany, easy to dip into, where town and country, home and abroad, meet in verse and brief prose.
4777-strong-as-death:
Guy de Maupassant opens Strong as Death, part one, chapter one, called A Duel of Hearts, in an artist's studio. Broad daylight streams through a skylight, showing a large square of dazzling blue and flocks of birds in rapid flight across limitless azure. Yet glad light hardly enters the severe room, with high ceilings and draped walls. It grows soft and dim, slumbering among hangings and dying in portieres.

Dark corners hold gilded frames of portraits gleaming like flame, and peace and sleep seem imprisoned in an artist's dwelling where the human soul has toiled. Within walls where thought abides, struggles, and exhausts itself in violent efforts, everything appears weary once action abates, as if dead after life's great crises. Furniture, hangings, and unfinished portraits of personages share that weariness. Readers get a Maupassant novel of love, art, and ageing, opening in a studio heavy with beauty and fatigue.
4886-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
John of Barneveld, founder of the Dutch commonwealth, is the subject of this first volume of Motley's final history, and it opens with the advocate balancing church and state. Barneveld holds the Union of Utrecht together, compromises between civil officials and churchmen, and sends embassies to France, England, and Venice.

Trouble follows the appointment of Arminius as professor of theology at Leyden, while the Catholic League faces a great Protestant union abroad. The death of the Duke of Cleve then sparks a succession struggle, with Brandenburg and the Palatine holding the duchies on Barneveld's advice against the emperor. Motley presents a statesman building a republic through law, alliance, and patient negotiation.
4887-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
Henry IV of France's passion for Margaret de Montmorency drives this Barneveld volume into court scandal and near war. Her marriage to the Prince of Conde, the couple's flight to the Netherlands, and the king's rage draw in Spanish intriguers and the archdukes at Brussels, who receive the fugitives with ceremony.

Spinola entertains the Condes splendidly, De Coeuvres missions to Brussels try to bring them back, and the republic sits in a difficult position between a furious king and a scheming Spain. Motley follows the golden thread of a private obsession through vast secret preparations for war. The volume shows how a royal affair could nearly set Europe alight.
4888-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
Barneveld's diplomacy takes center stage in this volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows the advocate through insurrection at home and embassies abroad. The States' army puts down the Utrecht rising, while special embassies to England and France seek support against Spain and the archdukes.

In Paris, Dutch commissioners receive a brilliant reception, interview Henry and his ministers, and discuss the India trade, the corsair Simon Danzer, and preparations for war. Motley also notes Henry's anger with Spain and his wish for Barneveld's presence. The volume shows a republic whose survival depended as much on envoys' manners and timing as on soldiers' muskets.
4889-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
Dutch commissioners meeting King James open this Barneveld volume, and John Lothrop Motley uses the talks to show the republic's widening rifts. Maurice takes command of the troops, Julich surrenders, Matthias is crowned king of Bohemia, and Rudolph dies, while James dreams of a Spanish marriage for his son.

At Leyden, Vorstius replaces Arminius, and an interview between Maurice and Winwood sharpens the bitterness between Barneveld and the prince. Motley contrasts the colder Dutch councils with the feverish intrigue of France after Henry's murder. The volume traces a republic whose foreign policy and domestic quarrels were becoming one crisis.
4890-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
The condominium in the duchies of Julich and Cleves anchors this Barneveld volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows a shared rule that pleased almost no one. Neuburgers and Brandenburgers quarrel, Brandenburg troops occupy Julich with States-General help, and Spain and the archdukes protest the intrusion.

Spinola descends on Aix-la-Chapelle, takes Orsoy and other places, and Wesel surrenders, until a conference at Xanten permanently divides the territory between Brandenburg and Neuburg. Motley tracks the subsidies, delays, and Spanish prohibitions that dragged the settlement out. The volume shows Barneveld managing a German succession crisis that threatened to draw in all of Europe.
4891-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
Francis Aerssens, the Dutch ambassador to France, overstays his post in this Barneveld volume, and John Lothrop Motley shows the loose constitutional frame that let him do it. Holland appointed and paid him, though he served the whole republic, and his long stay brought him personal advantages that drew complaints.

Aubery du Maurier, the new French ambassador, demands Aerssens's recall, the Peace of Sainte-Menehould intervenes, and Langerac takes up the Paris post. Motley uses the episode to explain how the United Provinces actually governed abroad: through provincial purse strings and personal networks. The volume is a quiet study in early modern diplomacy's machinery.
4892-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
Barneveld as founder of the Dutch commonwealth is the theme of this volume, which John Lothrop Motley uses to explain how a republic governs itself. Maurice serves as stadholder yet remains servant to the States-General, the Union of Utrecht holds, and Barneveld brokers a compromise between civil officers and church officials.

Embassies go to France, England, and Venice, while Arminius's appointment to teach theology at Leyden stirs dissension that will outlast the volume. Abroad, a great Protestant union opposes the Catholic League, and the Cleves succession pits Brandenburg and the Palatine against the emperor. Motley portrays state-building as daily negotiation, not a single founding act.
4893-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
Barneveld's alarm across Germany returns in this volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows the advocate's efforts to rally Protestant Europe. Langerac carries his instructions, the Prince Palatine's forces take Aachen and Mulheim, and Austrian and League activity grows while Protestant princes hesitate.

Barneveld presses England for help and finds James slippery over a proposed treaty, his influence running stronger in France than in London. Neuburg leaves for Germany, Mansfield takes service with Savoy, and Brandenburg faces citation. Motley portrays an elder statesman working every channel at once, against allies whose promises outran their deeds.
4894-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
Bohemia's defenestration opens this Barneveld volume, and John Lothrop Motley treats it as the real beginning of the Thirty Years' War. Ferdinand of Gratz is crowned king of Bohemia. He hates Protestants. His officials Slawata and Martinitz are thrown from the windows of the Hradschin. Europe then slides toward a war of faith and empire.

The Elector Palatine plots against Austria and backs Savoy. He draws in rival princes. Emperor Matthias visits Dresden, and Protestants mark the Reformation's hundredth year. Motley opens with the aged Rudolph signing away a crown in helpless rage. The volume links Dutch politics to a continental crisis Barneveld could neither control nor escape.
4895-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
Maurice's revolution of the provinces in 1618 dominates this Barneveld volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows the stadholder town by town. Nymegen, recovered from Spain a generation earlier, holds its government at the prince's option, and Maurice moves to secure provinces he cannot yet fully rely on.

A libellous pamphlet by Danckaert, Barneveld's appeal to the prince, and his remonstrance to the States frame the political fight, while the Treaty of Truce nears expiry. Spain and Archduke Albert watch for a chance to recover the provinces, and a secret plot aims to make Maurice sovereign. Motley shows a republic sliding from quarrel toward coup.
4896-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
Religious rancor inside the republic dominates this late Barneveld volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows the parties toward a breaking point. While Barneveld hides from public sight, Gomarist and Arminian factions harden, Spanish intrigues exploit the split, and James of England shifts inconsistently between them.

At Leyden, Brewster and Robinson's congregation decides to leave for America, hearing Robinson's farewell sermon and prayer at parting. Motley sets that quiet departure against a dark winter of faction and foreign meddling. Readers see how a theological quarrel became a political crisis, and how one congregation chose exile over submission.
4897-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
Barneveld's execution closes his story in this volume, and John Lothrop Motley narrates the advocate's conduct on the scaffold with sober attention. The sentence, printed and sent to the provinces, followed proceedings Motley calls irregular and inequitable, and the Hague's old castle quarter forms the somber backdrop.

The narrative pauses on the town itself, its brown brick ranges picked out with white stone, before returning to the trial's flaws and the advocate's bearing. Motley treats the execution as a political act with lasting stain, not a lawful end to a quarrel. Readers finish the Barneveld story understanding why Dutch memory kept the advocate's name alive.
4898-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
Barneveld sounds the alarm across Germany in this volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows the advocate as Protestantism's prime minister. Instructions go to Langerac, the Prince Palatine's forces take Aachen, Mulheim, and other towns, and Protestant supineness meets rising Austrian and League activity.

Barneveld seeks help from England, where James proves slippery over a new treaty, and finds his influence greater in France than in London. Neuburg departs for Germany, Mansfield serves Savoy, and the Elector of Brandenburg faces citation to appear. Motley shows an aging statesman trying to rally a divided cause before war engulfs it, with allies who promise more than they deliver.
4941-the-house-boat-boys-or-drifting-dow:
Two boys meet at a country post office below Evansville, Indiana, in this house-boat adventure, and their friendship carries the story south. Maurice, better dressed and refined, and Thad Tucker, rougher in manner, are the closest of chums despite their differences, sharing joys and disappointments as they drift downriver.

A letter from a tramp steamer sets their journey in motion, toward the sunny south promised by the title. The record carries no author byline. Readers get a boys' river tale of boats, scrapes, and loyalty, in the tradition of stories where the river itself teaches its travelers how to grow up.
5106-the-canadian-brothers-or-the-prophe:
Major John Richardson's Canadian Brothers opens its first volume at Amherstburg, the small fortress at the northern extremity of its town at the head of Lake Erie. It is the summer of 1812, and intelligence has arrived that the United States has declared war, aiming at the conquest and incorporation of provinces long eyed with political jealousy.

England, fighting in Europe, faces an American attack at a moment of distraction, and the fortress prepares for a war that will test Canadian loyalty. Richardson, who served in the country, writes with a soldier's knowledge. Readers get the opening volume of a War of 1812 romance, where prophecy and frontier warfare intertwine.
5107-the-canadian-brothers-or-the-prophe:
The Canadian Brothers continues a frontier tale of the War of 1812 era, opening as an American party sails toward Buffalo under the command of the young officer Gerald. Its chapters follow soldiers, settlers, and their families through the border country of lakes and forts, where an old prophecy is said to shape the fate of two brothers.

Love, loyalty, and wartime danger drive the plot, with captures, escapes, and family secrets along the way. The novel gives readers a romantic view of early Canadian and American frontier life. It was written when memories of the war were still fresh and the border itself was newly drawn.
5108-the-canadian-brothers-or-the-prophe:
Major John Richardson's Canadian Brothers, in complete form, gathers the whole tale of the prophecy fulfilled. It opens at Amherstburg in the summer of 1812. It follows the War of 1812's campaigns and consequences. The fortress at the head of Lake Erie anchors the opening. The American declaration of war follows. The aim of conquering Canada drives the plot.

Prophecy, loyalty, and frontier warfare carry the narrative across its full length, with Richardson's soldier knowledge grounding every march and siege. Readers who want the complete romance, rather than the first volume alone, get the Canadian Brothers entire, in the form that lets the prophecy run its full course.
5117-the-meaning-of-truth:
William James wrote The Meaning of Truth as a sequel to Pragmatism, gathering essays that defend his account of truth against critics. At the centre stands his claim. An idea is true when it agrees with reality in ways that can be tested, checked, and lived with, rather than when it merely copies reality in the mind.

Essays on humanism, the knower and the known, and even the existence of Julius Caesar press the argument from different angles. James answers professors Pratt and Hebert and other misunderstanders with patience and bite. The book remains the clearest statement of how pragmatism handles one of philosophy's oldest questions.
5425-the-five-books-of-youth:
Robert Hillyer gathered his early poems into five books under the title The Five Books of Youth. Many of the pieces had first appeared in magazines such as The Nation, The New Republic, and The Dial, and Hillyer thanks their editors for permission to reprint them. The five books move through miscellany, days and seasons, and other groupings of short lyrics.

Poems like La Mare des Fees, Prothalamion, and Thermopylae show a young poet working in traditional forms, writing about love, landscape, memory, and classical subjects. Readers get a portrait of an American lyric voice finding its range, poem by poem, in the years before Hillyer became better known.
5606-guns-of-the-gods-a-story-of-yasmini:
Talbot Mundy wrote Guns of the Gods as a story of Yasmini's youth, set in princely India. Yasmini herself demands that her thoughts, not the narrator's, be set down if the tale is to be worth the pesa. Chapter headings carry her voice: gold is where you find it, friendship's friendship but duty's what I'm paid to do, and the law is like a python after monkeys in the treetops.

The story follows Yasmini, soldiers, elephants, and a Maharajah, with Gungadhura's fate closing in and discretion urged as the better part of secrecy. Readers get an Indian adventure of intrigue and loyalty, told with Mundy's pace and color.
6-give-me-liberty-or-give-me-death:
Virginia patriots debated war or patience in Richmond in March 1775. Patrick Henry rose to argue that delay had become a form of slavery. His speech closes with the famous choice between liberty and death.

Henry warns against illusions of hope and pleads for plain truth about British intent. He counts the colonies' strength in numbers, arms, and cause, not in British mercy. The speech pushed Virginia toward armed resistance. Its final line became a rallying cry for the Revolution. Reprinted in schoolbooks for generations, the speech still fires debates about courage under threat.
6091-senator-north:
Gertrude Atherton opens Senator North with a Senate voice warning that a new member, however eminent elsewhere, has much to learn and much to endure. He may know public affairs well, yet not grasp the difficulties that embarrass every effort to make knowledge useful.

Upright in purpose and strong in belief in his own integrity, he still cannot dream of the ordeal ahead. Daily temptations, undeserved censure to control, and the contest between desire for public approbation and a sense of public duty await him. Atherton sets a Washington novel on that hard schooling.
6107-the-truth-about-jesus-is-he-a-myth:
M. M. Mangasarian asks whether Jesus is a myth, opening with Huxley's question: if it is not historically true that such things happened in Palestine eighteen centuries ago, what becomes of Christianity? His contents state the problem, weigh Christian documents, virgin births, the cross's origin, and the silence of contemporary writers.

Later parts ask whether the world is indebted to Christianity, whether it suits western races, and what modern voices say, from a rhetorical Jesus to a liberal Jew praising him. An appendix answers clerical critics. Mangasarian writes as a skeptic testing scripture against history, plainly and combatively.
6628-the-life-crime-and-capture-of-john-:
George Alfred Townsend, a special correspondent, tells the life, crime, and capture of John Wilkes Booth, with a full sketch of the plot he led. The pursuit, trial, and execution of his accomplices fill out the tale, which opens with a curious note on relics of Waterloo. Townsend, like a reporter on the spot, gathers journals, dispatches, and gossip of the day.

Booth's deed, his flight, and his end are told with the detail of a man writing close to the event. The book reads as both news and history, vivid and grim. The Life, Crime, and Capture of John Wilkes Booth is a key early account of Lincoln's murder and the hunt that followed.
6713-god-s-answers-a-record-of-miss-anni:
Clara Lowe records Annie Macpherson's work at the Home of Industry in Spitalfields, London, and in Canada, under the title God's Answers. The text opens with a verse from Chronicles on peace to helpers. Chapters trace Macpherson from 1861 to 1869. They cover prayer meetings, a move from Cambridgeshire, work in the Bedford Institute, and a voyage to New York.

First girls and boys rescued, matchbox-makers aided, and a revival refuge opened for both sexes fill the early record. The Home of Industry, secured in 1868, anchors the work. God's Answers is a warm, earnest record of Victorian charity, emigration, and faith in action.
6846-my-lady-of-the-north:
Randall Parrish tells My Lady of the North, the love story of a gray jacket, opening with a despatch for Longstreet, a night ride, and an unwelcome guest. A woman with a temper, a disaster on the road, a struggle in the dark, and a disciple of Sir Walter follow, with Mrs. Bungay defending her hearthstone and a hero in enemy hands. A woman's tenderness, Sheridan's presence, and a sentence of death raise the stakes.

Through camps, battles in the Shenandoah, and a field hospital, love endures amid Civil War strife. Parrish writes with a romantic's verve for the Confederacy's cause. My Lady of the North is a stirring, old-style Civil War romance.
6860-keineth:
Jane Abbott dedicates Keineth to all the little girls she knows, opening as Keineth Randolph's world suddenly turns upside down. For three days, something has shifted, and chapters on her world changing, her decision, Overlook, and a letter to her father follow. Pilot comes to Overlook, music the fairies put in her fingers sounds, and Alice runs away.

A page from history, a captive maiden, Pilot in disgrace and winning a home, camping, tennis, school days, and Christmas fill the tale. Abbott writes with a girl's-eye warmth and humor. Keineth is a charming, old-style girls' book of a young musician finding her place.
6947-the-rangers-or-the-tory-s-daughter-:
D P Thompson, author of The Green Mountain Boys, turns in this tale to the revolutionary history of Vermont and the northern campaign of 1777. He had meant to include Bennington and the older southern parts of the state in his former work, but found the ground too wide for one book's unity. After ten years he took up the deferred design, drawing on rich materials his research had gathered.

Two volumes in one, in a tenth edition, the novel follows the Rangers and a Tory's daughter through a border war of raids, loyalties, and divided homes. Thompson writes as a Vermonter proud of his state's part in the Revolution. The book mixes adventure with history, giving fiction to events his earlier work had left aside.
6997-the-winning-of-barbara-worth:
Harold Bell Wright tells the winning of Barbara Worth against the reclamation of the Colorado Desert, now the Imperial Valley. His acknowledgment stresses the story is neither a history of that region nor a biography. Yet the work of the past ten years, turning a vast desolate waste into homes, cities, and farms, inspired it. He thanks engineers and surveyors of the reclamation, business friends, pioneer ranchers, and William Mulholland.

Barbara herself, often pictured gazing over the great basin, longs to know the secret it holds. The novel that follows joins desert, water, and human will, as engineers tame a waste and a young woman finds her place in it. Wright writes a popular romance of the new West, built on real labor and real hope.
7020-louis-agassiz-as-a-teacher-illustra:
Lane Cooper, professor of English at Cornell, gathers illustrative extracts on Louis Agassiz as a teacher, with an introductory note. A Lowell verse at the head praises the teacher whose better self lives on in minds he touched with fire, and whose living word still stirs the air. Cooper answers why a teacher of English should issue a book on a naturalist: he was taught, and tries to teach, by a method in essence the same as Agassiz used.

The extracts show Agassiz training eyes to truth's exact severity, through close looking rather than book learning alone. Loving scholars in endless file, Lowell promises, will share the glow of his transmitted touch. The volume is a tribute to teaching by observation, from a humanist who learned from a scientist.
7055-gone-to-earth:
Mary Webb's Gone to Earth opens in the Callow, a spinney of silver birches and larches topping a round hill. Small feckless clouds hurry across a vast untroubled sky, torn to fragments on mountain fangs, leaving only a few tears. Cold air, purple mist hinting buds, and a fainter purple in the vistas mark a spring still half fledged, hopping tentatively through undergrowth like a young bird.

Only the sharp calyx point and pricking tip of the bud show as yet, not the paten of leaf or chalice of flower. Bright springing mercury carpets the open spaces of the wood. Webb writes the Shropshire hills with a poet's eye, and the novel that follows joins a wild girl, a fox, and the pull of earth and passion.
7122-the-emigrant-mechanic-and-other-tal:
Thomas Cowherd offers The Emigrant Mechanic and other tales in verse, with numerous songs upon Canadian subjects. His preface feels little apology needed, though the world floods with rhyme on every subject, most of it mediocre. Though he lived only a short time on a bush farm, his experiences were practical enough to speak with confidence on rural matters. His strongly expressed religious opinions rest on careful study of God's word.

To learning he makes only slender pretensions, having been born in a humble rank and gone to his trade at the start of his teens. Seven long years at weary hours left little chance for study, yet verse became his voice. The tales and songs that follow speak of emigration, bush life, and faith, in a workingman's plain rhyme.
7386-egyptian-tales-translated-from-the-:
Long before the modern novel, Egyptians were already telling stories, and W. M. Flinders Petrie, the great excavator, translated some of the oldest surviving ones here. This first series covers the Fourth through Twelfth Dynasties, in a second edition published in 1899. Petrie worked directly from the papyri, with illustrations by Tristram Ellis.

The tales include the magicians at Khafra's court, the peasant and the workman, the shipwrecked sailor, and the adventures of Sanehat. Petrie's introduction argues that the growth of fiction itself can be traced in them: from simple marvels to contrasts of town and country, Egypt and foreign lands, and personal character. The book is a window onto the oldest literature in the world, still fresh after four thousand years.
7429-trials-and-triumphs-of-faith:
Mary Cole tells her own life story as a story of faith tested and answered. She describes herself as once doomed to be only a burden to herself and her friends, until God took her, healed her, and fitted her for service. How she was then used as an instrument for his glory is the subject of the book.

The preface sets her life beside lives of greater public fame, from Washington and Gladstone to Joan of Arc, arguing that any life shaped by conviction is worth relating. Cole's account is plain and earnest, written for readers who look for encouragement in their own trials. It belongs to the Victorian tradition of spiritual autobiography, in which suffering becomes the ground of usefulness.
7550-quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of:
George Meredith's novels, from The Ordeal of Richard Feverel to his mature work, are gathered here in short passages and pictures. Portraits show him at thirty-five, sixty-eight, and eighty, with his sitting room at Flint Cottage. Readers long found his prose both dazzling and hard to follow. The passages are chosen to show why, in brief compass.

Read together, they sketch a novelist alert to self-deception in love and in polite society. Lovers, talkers, and would-be wise men all get sharp treatment. The passages reward slow reading, since a single sentence often turns an idea inside out. It is a good first taste of Meredith: demanding, witty, and keen on the gap between what people claim and what they do.
770-the-story-of-the-treasure-seekers-be:
E. Nesbit wrote this tale of the Bastable children, who set out to find a fortune and restore their family's luck. Oswald, the narrator, leads his brothers and sisters through a council of ways and means, with schemes ranging from digging for treasure to selling poetry. Each plan goes wrong in a funny, human way.

The children are brave, loyal, and gloriously impractical, and their failures teach them more than success would. Nesbit writes in a child's voice that is sly and warm at once. The book, dedicated to Oswald Barron, began the Bastable series and remains a beloved classic of family adventure.
7938-virgilia-or-out-of-the-lion-s-mouth:
Felicia Buttz Clark published Virgilia, or Out of the Lion's Mouth, in 1917 as a story of faith in ancient Rome. Its heroine is a young Christian girl living under an emperor the book calls one of the cruellest Rome ever suffered. Chapters move from a confession of faith and the hymn of a water-carrier to the circus. Where a crowd of a hundred thousand watches gladiators in the arena, and to the coming of Lycias the gladiator.

The novel mixes adventure with devotion, asking what courage faith requires when the state demands worship of its own gods. Written for young readers, it keeps its scenes vivid and its moral clear. It belongs to a popular tradition of Christian historical fiction, and it still offers a dramatic doorway into Rome's arenas and its early Christian communities.
8068-expositions-of-holy-scripture-deute:
Alexander Maclaren, D. D. , Litt. D. , preached these expositions on Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, First Samuel, Second Samuel, and First and Second Kings through chapter seven. His sermon titles show his method: God's Faithfulness, The Lesson of Memory, The Eating of the Peace-Offering, Prophets and the Prophet, A Choice of Masters, and The Spirit of the Law. Each exposition takes one passage and draws out its meaning for ordinary Christian life.

Maclaren was one of the great Victorian preachers, and his expositions read like sermons meant to be used, not just admired. They move steadily through the Old Testament narrative, pausing at scenes of choice and failure. For readers who want to study these books with a trusted guide, the volume offers clear, warm, and practical commentary.
8137-the-girls-of-central-high-aiding-th:
Gertrude W. Morrison wrote this Central High story about schoolgirls aiding the Red Cross through amateur theatricals for a worthy cause. Its chapters promise mystery and fun: the oddest thing that ever happened, the Red Cross girl, a mystery man, sand in the gears. A bank-note, an ice carnival, rehearsals, bubble and poetry, ember night, a startling announcement, and the case for and against Purt. The girls' play becomes the centre of school and town effort.

The novel belongs to the girls' series tradition, mixing school life, friendship, and wartime service. Its heroines learn organisation, courage, and teamwork while putting on a show. For young readers and collectors of series fiction, it is a cheerful wartime story of girls doing their bit.
8160-recollections-of-my-childhood-and-y:
George Brandes, author of a study of William Shakespeare, wrote these recollections of his childhood and youth in Denmark. His sections trace discovering the world, first impressions, going to bed, his name, school, the king, town and country. The king's gardens, the theatre, progress, and warlike instincts, then boyhood's years, his house and its inmates, and both grandfathers. A producer's note warns that sub-headings in the second longer stay abroad skip from seven to nine in the original.

Brandes, the great Danish critic, writes with the same sharp observation that marked his literary work. His Copenhagen childhood, with its theatre, books, and family life, becomes a portrait of a mind forming. For readers of autobiography and Scandinavian literature, the book is a vivid and intelligent memoir.
8235-the-world-english-bible-web-ruth:
Ruth, in the World English Bible, opens in the days when the judges judged, with famine in the land. Elimelech of Bethlehem Judah takes his wife Naomi and sons Mahlon and Chilion to Moab, where he dies. The sons marry Orpah and Ruth, and after about ten years both sons die too, leaving Naomi widowed and childless. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book follows Ruth's loyalty, her return with Naomi, and her marriage to Boaz.

The modern version tells this short story with tenderness and clarity, so Ruth's famous pledge and the harvest scenes shine. Ruth here remains the Bible's gentlest narrative, about loyalty across peoples and the quiet workings of providence. For new readers, it is the perfect short book with which to begin the histories.
8462-the-man-in-gray-a-romance-of-north-:
Thomas Dixon, author of The Clansman and The Birth of a Nation, writes this romance of North and South. He dedicates it to his Kappa Alpha fraternity brothers, a group founded under the inspiration of Robert E Lee. The Man in Gray, illustrated with a child asking if papa will come back home from the war, tells a Civil War story from Dixon's Southern viewpoint.

Dixon's novels shaped how generations imagined Reconstruction, and this book shares their sympathies and their flaws. Readers should approach it as a period document: a popular Southern romance, influential and controversial. Its value lies in showing how the war's memory was written, not in balanced history.
8556-the-history-of-england-from-the-nor:
This volume comes from a series that set out to retell England's past with new tools. Its preface notes that seventy-five years had passed since Lingard's work, which stopped at the Revolution of 1688. In that span, study had grown, source hoards had grown, and fresh light had fallen on deeds and figures, and the series aimed to use it all.

The book starts with the Norman Conquest, in the sweep its title claims, and follows the realm's politics from records, in a style meant for wide reading. Readers get early twentieth-century history writing, learned and narrative at once. It suits those tracing England's political tale in a series built to serve a new age.
8648-war-poetry-of-the-south:
William Gilmore Simms edited this 1866 anthology of Southern Civil War poetry, published by Richardson and Company the year after the war ended. The poems speak for the Confederate cause, its soldiers, its losses, and its home front, and Simms dedicates the volume to the women of the South. He frames them as having lost a cause but shown a spirit worth recording.

Battle pieces, laments, and songs of endurance sit side by side, giving a chorus of wartime feeling rather than a single poet's view. Historians value the book as evidence of how the South first told its own war story in verse. Readers should approach it as a partisan document of its time, useful for understanding Southern memory, and for hearing the war's poetry beyond the Northern anthologies.
8747-wordsworth:
F. W. H. Myers writes this life of William Wordsworth, opening with verses about a gift won from worlds not quickened by the sun. An intermingling of heaven's pomp spread on ground British shepherds tread. Chapters follow birth and education at Cambridge, residence in London and in France, Miss Wordsworth and the Lyrical Ballads, and settlement at Grasmere. The English Lakes, marriage, society, a Highland tour, Sir George Beaumont, and the death of John Wordsworth follow.

Later chapters cover the Happy Warrior and patriotic poems, children and life at Rydal Mount with The Excursion, poetic diction, Laodamia, the evening ode. Natural religion, closing with an Italian tour and ecclesiastical sonnets. Myers, a sympathetic Victorian critic, traces how a revolutionary youth became the sage of the Lakes. The life remains a graceful short biography, ideal for readers meeting Wordsworth beyond the famous daffodils.
8872-report-on-the-condition-of-the-sout:
Carl Schurz reports on the condition of the South in this 1865 Senate document, first published as Senate Executive Document number two of the thirty-ninth Congress. President Johnson transmits it in compliance with a Senate resolution of December 12, sending information on the states lately in rebellion. Schurz's report on South Carolina, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana, and a report by Lieutenant General Grant on the same subject. It was read and ordered printed on December 19, 1865.

Schurz, a German-American general and reformer sent south by Johnson, travelled the defeated states and found white resistance to emancipation, Black Codes, and violence, contradicting rosier accounts. His frank findings helped shape Radical Reconstruction debates. Historians treat the report as a landmark primary source on the first months after Appomattox. Readers get a clear, unsparing view of a South deciding, painfully, what freedom would mean.
8881-a-fleece-of-gold-five-lessons-from-:
Charles Stewart Given draws five lessons from the fable of Jason and the Golden Fleece in this 1905 book, second edition revised, dedicated to his sons Kingsley and Gordon. An epigraph shows Jason and his men seizing the favourable moment of the rebound, plying oars with vigour, and passing through in safety. Contents list, among others, the ruling element and the ethics of activity, with Given's own name attached to the lessons.

The first lesson asks what constitutes a state, answering that it is not high battlements, thick walls, moated gates, proud cities, broad ports, or starred courts where low-browed baseness wafts perfume. Given turns the old myth into moral instruction for young men: courage, timing, teamwork, and character over display. Readers interested in Edwardian self-help and classical moralizing will find a short, earnest book, plain in style and confident in its classical examples.
8928-simo-n-boli-var-the-liberator-patri:
Guillermo A. Sherwell, a Mexican scholar and former rector of the National University of Mexico, wrote this life of Simón Bolívar, first printed in Washington in 1921. Bolívar, called the Liberator, led the wars that freed much of Spanish South America in the early 1800s, and is named father of five nations.

Sherwell traces Bolívar's youth, his campaigns, his statesmanship, and his sad last years, when the vast lands he freed split apart. The sketch is short and clear, meant for readers new to the hero. It still serves as a plain guide to a man whose name marks streets and states across a continent.
9568-the-frost-spirit-and-other-poems-pa:
Part one of volume two of Whittier's works opens his Poems of Nature, with The Frost Spirit at the head. The Frost Spirit, The Merrimac, Hampton Beach, and A Dream of Summer follow in a chain of New England scenes. Whittier, a Quaker poet, finds moral calm in woods, shores, and seasons. This part leads the nature group of his collected verse.

The opening run favors short lyrics over long tales, each tied to a place or a season. Frost, river, beach, and summer dream all serve as signs of a larger order. A reader gets Whittier at his most lyrical, with nature verse that is plain, devout, and easy to carry in mind.
9915-an-appeal-to-the-christian-women-of:
Angelina Emily Grimké, a South Carolina woman who had left the South, addressed this appeal to the Christian women of her home region in the 1830s. She calls on them to speak against slavery, quoting Esther's resolve to go before the king even if she perished.

Grimké argues that silence makes slaveholding women share in the sin, and that faith demands action rather than quiet disapproval. Her pamphlet became a landmark of abolitionist writing by a southern woman. Readers meet an urgent, Bible-grounded argument that helped move antislavery feeling in the North.
9941-biography-of-a-slave-being-the-expe:
Charles Thompson, a preacher of the United Brethren Church, published this account of his life as a slave in the South in 1875. He writes plainly that he is no book-maker and claims only truthfulness and honesty of purpose, hoping to do good to his own race and to all who read.

Thompson was born a slave in Atala County, Mississippi, near Kosciusko, and his story includes parting from his mother, a grief he mourns before their final separation. Later chapters follow his path to preaching and freedom. Readers get a rare firsthand slave narrative, told in a preacher's direct voice.
a-fleece-of-gold-five-lessons-from-the-f: Charles Stewart Given draws five lessons from the fable of Jason and the golden fleece. One lesson, the ethics of activity, asks what constitutes a state, answering that it is not walls, cities, or navies. Jason and his men seize the rebound of the waves and pass through in safety. Given turns the old myth into moral teaching for modern readers.
a-journey-into-the-interior-of-the-earth:
Jules Verne sends Professor Lidenbrock, his nephew Axel, and the guide Hans down into the earth, in Frederick Amadeus Malleson's translation, published by Ward, Lock in 1877 as the editor's note explains. The contents open with the professor and his family and a runic manuscript that poses a mystery to be solved at any price. The old document names an Icelandic crater as the door.

Forty-five chapters descend Sneffels, lose and find water, cross a vast underground sea by raft, and meet the remains of prehistoric life. Thalatta, thalatta, Axel cries at the shore. Verne mixes geology lessons with peril at every stage, and the return, through a volcanic eruption, is as wild as the descent.
a-lecture-on-the-preservation-of-health: Thomas Garnett lectures on the preservation of health in this pamphlet of 1800. Dedicated to Erasmus Darwin, it praises rude and sober life, labor, exercise, and temperance. Garnett argues that health repays the peasant's toil. The lecture offers plain medical counsel in the voice of its age. The short tract still speaks in a plain voice to modern readers.
a-social-history-of-the-american-negro-b: Benjamin Griffith Brawley writes a social history of the American Negro in 1921, treating the Negro problem in the United States together with a history and study of Liberia. The volume is dedicated to the memory of Norwood Penrose Hallowell, a Quaker-raised patriot whose father's house sheltered wounded Union soldiers and Charles Sumner. The volume joins American race history to the Liberian experiment. Its chapters carry a people from slavery toward self-determination.
a-woman-named-smith: Marie Conway Oemler tells of a woman named Smith in this 1919 novel, by the author of Slippy McGee. The frontispiece shows Sophy told that the lost key of Hynds House has been found, and the first chapter is called The Scarlet Witch Departs. A dedication in verse to Elizabeth Heyward Oemler recalls an awful baby soothed with Red Riding Hood, Mother Goose, Jack's beanstalk, and three little pigs. The story that follows is one where houses keep secrets and keys.
akbar-emperor-of-india-a-picture-of-life: Richard Garbe paints a picture of Akbar, emperor of India, and of sixteenth-century life and customs at his court. The study follows the ruler's policy of tolerance, his administration, and the daily world of palace, camp, and city. Drawing on Indian sources, Garbe presents Akbar as a statesman whose curiosity and fairness set him apart among rulers of his age.
amphitryo-asinaria-aulularia-bacchides-c: Titus Maccius Plautus appears in this volume of Roman comedies, translated by Paul Nixon, with Amphitryon, the Comedy of Asses, the Pot of Gold, the Two Bacchises, and the Captives. The plays turn on twins, tricks, lost gold, and mistaken identity, in the broad, farcical manner of ancient Rome. Nixon's version keeps their speed and comic bite for modern readers.
an-appeal-to-the-christian-women-of-the-: Angelina Emily Grimké appeals to the Christian women of the South, urging them to oppose slavery on grounds of faith and conscience. In its third edition, the appeal speaks directly to Southern women as moral agents able to act. Grimké's tract is a landmark of abolitionist and early feminist writing in America.
andy-the-acrobat-or-out-with-the-greates: Peter T. Harkness sends Andy the acrobat out with the greatest show on earth, drawing on chimpanzee hunters, circuses old and new, and how a great show travels. The book follows circus life from town to town, with its performers, animals, and hardships. Young readers get a backstage tour of the big top in its heyday.
apollonius-conic-sections-heath:
Thomas L. Heath published his edition of Apollonius's Conic Sections in 1896. Apollonius of Perga, called the Great Geometer, worked around 200 BCE. His Conics became the definitive ancient work on its subject.

Slice a cone at different angles and the curves appear. Circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas all arise from that single cut. Apollonius worked out their properties in propositions of great difficulty. His names for the curves still serve mathematics today. Kepler's astronomy and Newton's physics later depended on this theory. Heath's translation made the peak of ancient geometry readable in English. Few ancient scientific works waited so long for their full vindication.
bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-church-o:
The Reverend Thomas Perkins wrote this account of St Albans Cathedral and its abbey for Bell's series, with fifty illustrations. Perkins, rector of Turnworth in Dorset, had already written the series volumes on Rouen, Amiens, and Wimborne. His St Albans pairs the fabric's description with a short history of the abbey, from Offa's foundation legend to the great church that became a cathedral in the nineteenth century.

The retro-choir receives detailed treatment. Several altars once stood there. Our Lady of the Four Tapers stood under the east window, with an aumbry and triple-arched piscina in the south wall. That altar has since been restored, its upper part entirely new. St Michael's altar answered it on the north, with St Edmund's nearby. Perkins catalogues shrines, screens, and the wooden figure of a mendicant with a parish priest's patience and a camera-age eye.
beltane-the-smith:
Jeffery Farnol published this medieval romance in 1915, dedicating it to Frederick Hughson Hawley, to whom Beltane was no stranger. Arthur E. Becher illustrates. Beltane, a giant smith reared in the greenwood by the hermit Ambrose, comes out of the forest to face Black Ivo. The duke's tyranny fills Belsaye with instruments of pain. Chapter heads in the old style tell how love came to him in the greenwood, and of Helen the Proud.

A sampled scene shows Sir Gui's seat of judgment. A massy post with chains and iron girdle gleams red at sunset. A gilded chair on a dais waits for watching justice done on the duke's enemies. Citizens blench; country folk push closer. Farnol writes deliberate archaism — thee, thou, and hight — in the service of a Robin Hood-like rising led by a smith who is secretly nobly born.
bennett-deacon-skidmore-s-letters-writte:
D. M. Bennett, the freethought publisher, issued these comic letters in New York in 1879, presenting them as written for his paper The Truth Seeker by Joel Skidmore. Skidmore is billed as first deacon of the Zion Hill Baptist Church in New Jersey. His first letter, dated July 1878, confesses ten days of feeling it his bounden duty to write and give the editor the truth as it is in Jesus.

The joke runs on spelling and outrage. Skidmore has seen two or three of the infidel sheets and finds them simply horribl. His phonetic thunder rolls on toward the mansion he hopes is prepared for him in the New Jerusalem. It rolls, too, toward his dread of the other road, to regions of darkness and terror. Bennett, prosecuted for his freethought publishing, lets a deacon hang orthodoxy with its own rope of bad spelling.
biography-of-a-slave-being-the-experienc:
The Reverend Charles Thompson published this narrative in 1875, telling his experiences as a preacher of the United Brethren Church while still a slave in the South. His preface claims no literary attainments and asks to be judged on truthfulness and honesty of purpose alone. Acquaintances, he says, called for the book; members of his church, white as well as coloured, are asked to help its sale.

Hirings and partings structure the life. When a building job ends, Thompson is to return to Mr. Dansley and stay as long as he is wanted; instead he is taken off at once by Wilson, bidding farewell to the plantation people with a sad heart. He pauses to teach Northern readers that a grocery in the South means something far different — a dram shop. Startling occurrences incidental to slave life, says the title, and the narrative keeps the promise plainly.
black-and-white-land-labor-and-politics-:
Timothy Thomas Fortune published this study of the South in 1884, on land, labour, and politics. Fortune, the leading Black journalist of his generation, bases his conclusions on personal knowledge of southern classes and on ample published data. His preface argues that the labouring classes of any country pay all the taxes in the last analysis. Legislators, corporations, and syndicates systematically victimise them, in his account.

Wealth's other face gets a set-piece description. Fortune enters a venerable Black man's home, furnished in the richest modern style, where a hundred guests in beautiful attire celebrate his seventy-second birthday. The host had made his money since the war and told, indirectly, what he was worth. Such success, Fortune insists, must become general: land ownership and fair labour terms for the freedpeople, argued a decade before Washington's Atlanta Compromise set narrower terms.
bradford-plymouth:
William Bradford, governor of Plymouth Colony for most of his life, wrote his history of the plantation between 1630 and 1650. The manuscript stayed in family hands, vanished during the Revolution, and resurfaced in England. It is America's founding memoir.

Bradford tells how the Separatists fled England for Holland, then crossed on the Mayflower in 1620. He describes the first winter's deaths, the treaty with Massasoit, and the colony's slow growth. His plain style carries deep faith and quiet grief. The famous line about one small candle lighting a thousand comes from these pages. The manuscript's return to Massachusetts in 1897 was greeted as a homecoming.
britannica-1911-aberystwyth:
Aberystwyth receives a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The Cardiganshire borough and seaport stands where the Ystwyth and Rheidol meet near Cardigan Bay's middle. Rail ends here for the Cambrian and the Manchester and Milford lines.

A pier and a fine sea-front from Constitution Hill make it the west Welsh coast's most popular watering-place, the entry holds. The University College of Wales, raised in 1872, gives the town an education trade, and the Welsh National Library site was fixed here in 1905. Strongbow's fort of 1109 and Edward the First's castle of 1277 open the history. Owen Glendower held the castle from 1404 to 1408. Parliament's men razed it in 1647.
britannica-1911-adams-andrew-leith:
Andrew Leith Adams (1827-1882) was a Scottish naturalist and palaeontologist. He was born on the twenty-first of March 1827. Medicine was the profession chosen for him. He served as an army surgeon from 1848. The Army Medical Department posted him widely abroad. India, Kashmir, Egypt, and Malta hosted his service. Gibraltar and Canada completed the list. He used every posting for natural history.

Fossils claimed his mature attention. Malta's fossil vertebrates drew his first studies there. Fossil elephants then became his specialty. He became an acknowledged authority on them. The Royal Society elected him fellow in 1872. Dublin made him professor of zoology in 1873. Cork gave him its natural history chair in 1878. He died at Queenstown in 1882.
britannica-1911-aldrich-nelson-wilmarth:
Nelson Wilmarth Aldrich rose from Rhode Island local politics to long power in the United States Senate. Born at Foster in November 1841, he joined the Providence common council in 1869 and presided over it in 1871 and 1872. Next came the state lower house, where he was speaker by 1876.

A strong figure in state Republican politics, Aldrich won election to Congress in 1878 and again in 1880, then moved to the Senate early in his second term. Voters returned him in 1886, 1892, 1898, and 1905. Colleagues saw him as the voice of protected industry and wealthy interests. Tariff, banking, and merchant marine laws bore his mark most.
britannica-1911-aliwal-north:
Sulphur springs run through the streets of Aliwal North, a South African town where the Orange River's south bank runs. The town stands 4,300 feet above the sea and 282 miles by rail from the port of East London. In 1904 it held 5,566 people, 1,758 of them white. Trade and farming for the north-east Cape and for nearby parts of Basutoland and the Orange Free State centre there.

Good stone buildings and tree-lined roads give the town a pleasant face. Spring water flows down the streets in open runs. A stone bridge of 860 feet spans the river, which forms the border with the Orange Free State. The springs, a mile off, pour out more than 500,000 gallons a day and draw folk with rheumatic pain and skin ills. A dry, brisk climate pulls in those with weak chests as well, and quarries work the stone nearby.
britannica-1911-arbroath:
Arbroath is a seaport burgh of Forfarshire, Scotland. Aberbrothock is its fuller older name. It stands at the Brothock water's mouth. Dundee lies seventeen miles south-west. Population was 22,398 in 1901. A provost, bailies, and council govern it. It returns one member to parliament jointly. Brechin, Forfar, Inverbervie, and Montrose share that member. Industries lead with sailcloth and canvas manufacture.

Coarse linens, tanning, and boot-making follow. Bleaching, engineering, and shipbuilding operate there. Iron foundries and chemical works add variety. The harbour has a long improvement history. Abbots originally built and maintained it. An agreement of 1394 governed that arrangement. A more commodious harbour replaced it in 1725. Enlargements followed in 1844. A signal tower links to Bell Rock lighthouse. That lighthouse stands twelve miles south-east.
britannica-1911-azimuth:
Azimuth, a word from the Arabic, serves in astronomy. It is the angular distance from the horizon's north or south point to the foot of a vertical circle. That circle passes through a heavenly body. In plain terms, it measures how far around the horizon a star's direction sits from due north or south.

The term also serves on the ground. For a horizontal line, the azimuth is that line's deviation from the north or south direction, the angle by which it leans away from the meridian. One word thus covers both a star's place against the sky and a survey line's bearing on earth, each fixed by its angle from the north-south line.
britannica-1911-barmouth:
Barmouth, in Welsh Abermaw, meaning mouth of the Maw or Mawddach, is a small seaport on the north side of that river's estuary in Cardigan Bay, North Wales. It is the only haven in Merionethshire. Its urban district held 2,214 people in 1901, and the Cambrian railway serves it.

The town is a favourite bathing place and a summer centre for coaching tours, above all toward the Vale of Llangollen, and the ride to Dolgellau is praised as fine. The parish church of Llanaber stands a mile and a half away on a cliff over the sea. The 1911 Britannica entry is short, keeping to the port, the bathing, and the coaching trade.
britannica-1911-barry-elizabeth:
Elizabeth Barry (1658–1713), an English actress, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography that begins by admitting how little is known of her early life. She failed on stage at first and was more than once dismissed. Her lover, the earl of Rochester, then coached her, having bet that he could make a first-rate actress of her in a short time, and the wager proved sound.

Success in Mustapha delighted Charles II and the duke and duchess of York. Barry is said to have created more than a hundred parts, shining above all in the plays of Thomas Otway. Betterton and Dryden praised her acting in strong terms. Benefits, stage performances held for one person's profit, were first granted to an actor for her sake under James II. She retired in 1709 and died in November 1713.
britannica-1911-barth:
Barth, a town in Prussia in Germany, stands on the Barther Bodden, a lake connecting with the Baltic Sea, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica account. It lies fifteen miles north-west of Stralsund by rail. Its population in 1900 was 7070. The town's notable building is St Mary's, a fine Gothic Protestant church from the thirteenth century. Barth also had several schools, among them a school of seamanship training boys for life at sea.

Work in Barth mixed land and water trades. Its industries included iron-founding, shipbuilding, and brewing, plus the making of cigars, leather, and tinned fish. Grain was exported actively through the town. Taken together, the church, the seamanship school, the shipyards, and the grain trade give a compact picture of a small Baltic port town at the start of the twentieth century.
britannica-1911-barton-benjamin-smith:
Benjamin Smith Barton (1766–1815), an American naturalist born at Lancaster, Pennsylvania, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied for two years at Edinburgh and then graduated at Göttingen in Germany. Settling in Philadelphia, he soon built a considerable medical practice. Chairs followed at the College of Philadelphia, later the University of Pennsylvania. He taught botany and natural history from 1789, then materia medica, the study of medicines, and practical medicine after Benjamin Rush's death in 1813.

Honours and books complete the short entry. Barton was chosen president of the American Philosophical Society in 1802 and was one of its strong supporters. He wrote various works on natural history, botany, and materia medica. Among them, his Elements of Botany of 1803 is named as the best known. Barton died at Philadelphia on 19 December 1815, still in the city where he had spent his whole working life as doctor, teacher, and naturalist.
britannica-1911-barton-elizabeth:
Elizabeth Barton (about 1506–1534), known as the Maid of Kent, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry that treats her as a fraud. A servant girl near Aldington in Kent, she suffered epilepsy and, during illness at nineteen, fell into long trances. In them she rebuked sin with what country people took for inspired holiness. Archbishop Warham had her examined, and she entered St Sepulchre's convent at Canterbury as a nun.

Prophecy turned political and dangerous. Guided by the monk Edward Bocking, Barton claimed direct contact with the Virgin Mary.
